talks.title: Ai, Deception And Deepfakes When Trust Becomes The Primary Attack Surface
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Ai, Deception And Deepfakes When Trust Becomes The Primary Attack Surface.
talks.summary:
Overview: A nullcon panel explores AI, deception, and deepfakes as emerging attack surfaces where trust itself becomes the primary vulnerability across fintech, insurance, transport, and national security sectors.

Key Topics: Deepfake-enabled fraud in regulated sectors; North Korean synthetic identity infiltration of US companies and universities; trust erosion in hiring and authentication; and balancing AI defensive capabilities against offensive deception campaigns.

Technical Details: Panelists discuss how AI-generated synthetic identities undermine background checks and hiring pipelines. The fintech representative highlights critical infrastructure implications while the ex-military panelist frames threats from a national security perspective.

Takeaways: Deepfakes attack the trust layer underlying business operations and national security. Organizations in regulated sectors need multi-factor identity verification beyond document checks and video interviews.

talks.title: Cloud Resilience Simplified Less Data, Stronger Security
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Cloud Resilience Simplified Less Data, Stronger Security.
talks.summary:
Cloud Resilience Framing

A nullcon panel explores cloud resilience through data minimization and simplified architecture. Moderators argue that reducing data volume shrinks attack surface, speeds recovery, and strengthens security—linking India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act to resilience rather than compliance alone.

Discovering Dark Data

Panelists define dark data as unclassified, uncorrelated information in blind spots—obsolete OneDrive files, forgotten test databases, and decommissioned microservice data without lifecycle plans. Discovery requires cataloging structured versus unstructured data and applying classification tags.

Developer and Security Practices

Recommendations include data minimization at collection, assigning data ownership accountability, and embedding legal-retention hooks in code. DLP solutions protect classified data, while architects must plan data lifecycle when modernizing to microservices.

Attacker Entry Points

From an offensive perspective, orphaned and shadow data often becomes the weakest link—not always directly internet-exposed but reachable through application or perimeter vulnerabilities, making forgotten datasets high-value targets.

talks.title: Demystifying Driver Research A Systematic Approach For Vulnerability Hunting
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Demystifying Driver Research A Systematic Approach For Vulnerability Hunting.
talks.summary:
Why Drivers Matter

Priyanu presents at Nullcon on hunting vulnerabilities in signed Windows kernel drivers whose IOCTL interfaces let user-mode code reach privileged operations—valuable for red teams disabling EDR and for defenders prioritizing risky drivers.

Beyond Random Fuzzing

He calls out the beginner fallacy of fuzzing every driver blindly. Most drivers are poor targets; a repeatable pipeline beats one-off luck, and he cites his first CVE and professional engagement using this approach.

Five-Step Pipeline

The workflow starts with mass driver collection from DriverPack, Internet Archive, and cabinet extraction tools. API import filtering finds IoCreateDevice and IoCreateSymbolicLink usage, then dynamic loading verifies a user-reachable device actually appears.

Manual Review

Filtered drivers undergo reverse engineering: inspect dispatch tables, follow IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL handlers, and hunt memory corruption bugs. Exploit development is out of scope; the goal is consistent zero-day discovery rather than isolated fuzz hits.

talks.title: Dpdpa In Action Designing A 72 Hour Breach Response That Actually Works
talks.teaser: A practical breach response starts with early identification and clear communication to the board and affected people.
talks.summary:
Regulatory focus

A Nullcon panel examines India's DPDP Act Section 8 and Rule 7, requiring data fiduciaries to notify data principals and the Data Protection Board when a personal-data breach occurs.

Cyber vs privacy incidents

INOX GFL group CISO contrasts triggers: ransomware/extortion calls versus media/public leak discovery. Core assets differ (infrastructure vs personal data), impacts differ (ransom vs penalties up to hundreds of crores), and owners differ (CISO vs DPO), though roles often overlap.

Reporting lens

Cyber incidents may fall under IT Act timelines; privacy incidents invoke DPDP/GDPR-style regimes with 72-hour notification expectations.

Proactive response

JSW Paints' Neelamani Sahu urges internal breach identification before public exposure, board notification, then principal communication in plain language covering what leaked, mitigation steps, and user actions. Public discovery means failed controls and reactive damage control rather than ideal playbook execution.

talks.title: Regulation, Resilience and Reality: How CXOs Navigate the Compliance Security Trade-Off
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Regulation, Resilience and Reality: How CXOs Navigate the Compliance Security Trade-Off.
talks.summary:
## Overview
A Nullcon CXO panel deliberately avoids scripted GPT-style answers, debating how executives balance regulation, resilience, and operational reality.

## Three Lines of Defense
Panelists frame security governance as business ownership (first line), risk and resilience practices (second), and audit (third). Several argue audit-at-the-end is too late in the AI transformation era—controls must shift into design and build phases.

## Human and Organizational Factors
Clear accountability across the business matters more than checkbox compliance. Burnout on security teams is itself a cyber risk. During incidents, fast, factual, honest communication can make or break response.

## Future Outlook
AI will reshape both offense and defense—automated phishing, deepfakes, and nation-state activity are accelerating. The panel urges merging assurance lines rather than treating compliance as a terminal gate.

talks.title: The Ciso Equation Authority, Accountability, And Survival In The Modern Enterprise
talks.teaser: Panelists debate how CISOs match responsibility to authority, track unseen assets, and win business backing for security.
talks.summary:
This panel discussion asks how the CISO role is changing as cloud, mobile, social platforms and AI reached enterprises, often pushed from the top down. The moderator frames the session around evolving threats and asks the two panelists, both long-serving security leaders, how CISOs should adapt and what they should look for when hiring. One panelist, from manufacturing, argues that a security leader must know where attackers may come from and which weaknesses exist, while keeping production running. A vulnerability can sometimes be tolerated for a short period, and presenting security as an enabler helps the business accept that.

A central thread is visibility. The panelists agree that a known vulnerability becomes a problem when the CISO does not know the asset carrying it, and they describe shadow IT, shadow AI and unseen cloud resources as common gaps. Another panelist describes contract clauses that require vendors to report vulnerabilities and suggest hardening measures until patches are released. The discussion then moves to whether CISOs must learn to review AI-written code, and to the imbalance where security leaders carry blame without matching authority, with the suggestion that expressing risk as a financial figure helps leaders decide.

The closing part covers budgets and stakeholders. The business ultimately pays for controls, so security leaders should bring the CIO, CFO and product owners in early, explain impact in terms each one values, and treat them as partners rather than opponents. The takeaway for practitioners is that accountability is easier to carry when risk is quantified, shared and agreed in advance.

talks.title: The Meltdown Moment Cve 2025 21533 A Speculative Store Bypass In Oracle Virtualbox
talks.teaser: Shows how speculative store bypass let a low-privilege VirtualBox guest leak host memory, with a recorded demo.
talks.summary:
The talk covers CVE-2025-21533, a speculative store bypass flaw in Oracle VirtualBox that the speakers reported to Oracle's security team. VirtualBox is presented as a type 2 hypervisor that runs on a host operating system, with guest machines reaching the host's CPU cores and memory through it. The speakers explain that performance-driven speculation in modern CPUs can let data be read before access checks complete, and they use a restaurant analogy to illustrate out-of-order execution and discarded predicted values.

The middle of the talk walks through load and store ordering, the load-store queue, memory disambiguation, and how page tables and the TLB translate guest virtual addresses to host physical ones. The attack is described at a high level: a branch misprediction drives speculative execution, and cache timing is used to infer the values. A pre-recorded demo shows a two-stage exploit. In the first stage, a guest user recovers a secret of about 30 characters held on the Windows host. In the second, the attack logs keystrokes of a password typed into another virtual machine. The speakers said the full exploit is withheld under disclosure policy.

On mitigation, Oracle assigned the CVE, advised limiting local system access, and pointed to a kernel parameter setting that disables speculative store bypass. The speakers said Microsoft and Azure had not yet confirmed whether the issue affects them. The takeaway is that speculative execution can expose sensitive data before permission checks finish, so software isolation alone does not stop such leaks.

talks.teaser: An XXE testing sequence for SOAP services, from WSDL inspection to data extraction, plus parser settings that block external entities.
talks.summary: The speaker explains how SOAP requests use XML and how parsers turn that input into application objects. Attendees learn the speaker’s testing sequence and suggested mitigations, such as disabling external entities and limiting parser access to files and networks.

talks.title: Volatility Meets Ai Transforming Linux And Windows Memory Forensics For Modern Threats
talks.teaser: Shows how retrieval-augmented generation and Volatility can automate memory forensics to spot fileless attacks.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem: fileless and in-memory attacks leave little on disk, manual workflows and signature-based tools struggle, and correlating raw dump artifacts slows incident response. The presenters, security researchers at Microsoft, propose an automated framework that pairs Volatility extraction with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and a language model.

A lab setup generated a Meterpreter payload on an attacker machine, ran it on an Ubuntu victim VM, and captured the memory. Volatility pulled network connections, process memory maps and suspicious strings, which were normalized, embedded and stored in a Qdrant vector database with metadata. A false-positive case showed benign Firefox traffic matching reverse-shell artifacts; indicator-based filtering and a hybrid score (dense 0.5, BM25 0.3, indicator similarity 0.2, Jaccard threshold 0.6) addressed it.

In the Windows demo, the pipeline flagged a process with suspicious threads and AFD socket handles, tied it to an outbound TCP connection on port 443, and ran YARA scans on the suspicious memory. The language model then produced a report with observed behaviour, IOCs, MITRE ATT&CK mapping, a classification with confidence score, and recommendations. The takeaway is that grounding the model in retrieved context and filtering on indicators reduces hallucinated conclusions; future work includes agents to replace manual normalization.

talks.title: No Cve For That Mapping Invisible Breach Paths Across The Ai Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Maps exposed AI services, vector databases, shared chat links and leaked API keys that open breach paths without any CVE.
talks.summary:
The talk covers AI exposure: AI-related components, interfaces, identities and data paths that end up reachable from the internet, often because a quick project was left open. The presenter says reachability is the real problem, not sophisticated attacks on models. Internet scans reportedly surfaced hundreds of critical AI exposures a day.

The walkthrough goes layer by layer. Exposed inference servers and orchestration dashboards let outsiders send prompts, load models or reach connected tools. Unauthenticated vector databases leak stored data and can be altered, and ML management dashboards such as MLflow can expose downloadable models. Gateway admin panels, such as Kong, may allow rate-limit bypass. Shared chat links, published models and leaked AI API keys can carry internal details, and web archives and Common Crawl can surface old shared conversations.

The presenter explains that traditional tools miss these paths because there is no CVE to match, and the traffic looks like normal authenticated use. Suggested defenses include limiting blast radius, applying least privilege to agents, locking down memory and retrieval, protecting and rotating keys, monitoring behaviour rather than signatures, controlling supply chains and running continuous exposure management.

talks.title: Scalable Third Party Risk Management With Ai Driven Automation
talks.teaser: A CISO panel weighs fourth-party exposure, sanctions outages, and automation that keeps vendor fleets auditable.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens with a simple analogy: buying a car without wipers mirrors accepting software when critical components come from suppliers you do not control. A practitioner recounts how an advisory about a compromised antivirus vendor seemed irrelevant until a payment-software supplier that used that product was affected, forcing a war-room decision to accept deliverables while sandboxing files for behavioral signs of the known incident rather than halting a live UPI gateway.

Panelists contrast older Excel-and-compliance vendor onboarding with API-driven dynamic risk assessment, emphasizing secure-by-design architecture, external self-hack assessments, identity controls, and visibility into fourth parties. They describe geopolitical shocks such as sanctions cutting office and email access for days, semiconductor and antivirus supply disruptions, and operational surprises when a mass-email subcontract exceeded capacity. New concerns include agentic SOC providers, DRM add-ins that exfiltrate protected content through internal APIs, and India’s DPDP obligations when vendors act as data processors.

Practitioners are urged to map third and fourth parties continuously, align recovery expectations with vendors, and combine continuous monitoring with hygiene inside service meshes—not only perimeter firewalls. The group closes on vendor selection trade-offs between large integrators and niche startups, framed around reasonable assurance, incident-response speed, and scalability, plus light rapid-fire choices on passwords, zero-days, and AI-driven unpredictability.

talks.title: The Hidden Cost Of Sanitization How Secure Parsing Can Introduce New Xss Attack Surfaces
talks.teaser: Shows how sanitizers can create new XSS by reshaping HTML, using parser differences between sanitizers and browsers.
talks.summary:
Sanitizers are often treated as a complete fix for cross-site scripting, but the talk argues that the transformations they perform can open new paths. Browsers repair malformed markup in order to render it, while sanitizers apply policy to a parsed tree, and the two parsers do not always agree. Serializing a sanitized DOM and parsing the resulting string again can yield a different tree. A nested form trick made one form disappear on reparsing, moving content into a MathML namespace where a style element became executable. Earlier DOMPurify releases had similar issues.

Three case studies came from an enterprise email platform that chained two back-end sanitizers with front-end regex rewriting. In the first, an @import rewrite closed a quote early, letting an SVG element escape an image tag. In the second, encoded attribute values were decoded when read back into an iframe, and a regex matched a src string inside an alt attribute. In the third, a team added @media handling that skipped serialization, so comment-split payloads rejoined during fragment parsing. Each sanitizer looked safe alone; the combined pipeline was not.

The talk closed with mitigations: reject input where possible, avoid regex rewriting in favor of syntax-tree parsing, and render untrusted output in sandboxed iframes. Teams should validate each layer alone and combined, and audit by comparing the sanitized DOM with the DOM a browser builds. A checklist covered multi-sanitizer policy consistency, SVG and MathML content, and structural mutation testing. The core takeaway was that every transformation adds risk.

talks.title: Unauthenticated Pre Pairing Gatt Write Vulnerability In Smartwatch Ecosystems
talks.teaser: Shows how budget smartwatches accept unauthenticated BLE GATT writes that let attackers push fake calls and alerts.
talks.summary:
The speakers open with a demo: during a flight they connected to a colleague's budget smartwatch without authentication and pushed a fake incoming call. They then cover Bluetooth Low Energy basics, explaining why it saves power, why a connection is not the same as pairing, and how GAP and GATT organize services, characteristics, handles and UUIDs. In this model the watch acts as the server and the phone as the client.

The researcher mapped handles and UUIDs by trial and error and found a vendor-specific UUID exposing a write-without-response property. A write can impersonate a chosen application by changing one identifier byte, while a text payload carries the content. Possible abuses include fake calls and notifications, injected alarms, triggering Find My Device, and resetting the watch. To find the cause, the researcher logged traffic with an Android snoop tool, found it in plain text, dumped firmware from the flash chip and reverse engineered it in Ghidra. Two vendor firmwares had different root causes, a property set without authentication and a bonding flag left at zero, but the same underlying flaw class.

The speakers frame this as a trust and attention failure rather than a broken encryption scheme, since no pairing or key exchange is bypassed. They say about 70% of smartwatches in the Indian market are affected, and that nearby attackers need only a simple app. Their takeaway is that vendors should block GATT writes until pairing and authentication complete, as higher-end watches already do.

talks.title: Choosing The Right Battles Ciso Leadership In A Time Of Constant Disruption1
talks.teaser: Two security leaders discuss how to set priorities, share accountability and cut noise as threats change fast.
talks.summary:
This fireside chat takes up how security leaders should choose their battles when regulation, AI and new threats make everything look critical. Rishi, CISO at HCL Tech, argues that priorities come from situational awareness of both the outside world and the organisation's own plans for new technology, along with knowing the internal and partner ecosystem well enough to frame risk in business terms. He says that with good visibility into crown jewels, teams can work through a stream of new vulnerabilities in sequence rather than treating each one as an emergency on day zero.

M. A. K. P. Singh, a former CISO of the Ministry of Power, described the need to collect complete logs from connected devices so attack paths can be traced, and a proposed central incident response team that would watch the SOCs of power-sector utilities. He said budgets are hard to win because boards expect a clear return, and that agentic AI in SOC automation is being adopted carefully in OT environments, with staff trained on live systems. On burnout, he pointed to a password stolen years earlier that was reused in a Jira server compromise at Jaguar Land Rover, where a basic password-policy check might have stopped the attack.

On accountability, both speakers agreed that security cannot rest with the CISO alone. Rishi suggested tiering AI use cases by business risk, from summarisation to decision support to fully autonomous systems, so business owners see the value of controls. In the rapid-fire round they named firefighting as a trap, identity as a priority, learning from others' attacks, asking for help early, and mean time to detection as a key metric. The closing message was to prioritise, reduce noise and build alliances rather than silos.

talks.title: Building The Three Lines Of Defense For 2026 And Beyond
talks.teaser: A panel explores how the three lines of defense adapt for cloud, AI, and faster business cycles without blocking innovation.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens from a familiar governance frame: the first line owns risk, the second oversees it, and the third audits it. Panelists push back on stereotypes that cast security leaders as blockers, arguing instead that chief information security officers should enable the business—comparable to protective details that must keep principals visible while managing real threats. Cloud-native architectures, microservices, and enterprise AI adoption are said to strain an annual-audit mindset and intensify overlap among risk, security, and privacy roles.

Practical recommendations center on board engagement, shared responsibility, and speaking in business terms. Vulnerabilities should be tied to financial impact; resilience metrics such as recovery time should matter more than raw counts of findings or incidents. The third line is expected to run continuously, aided by monitoring tools and threat intelligence, while auditors face harder questions when models make opaque decisions—bias, poisoning, and varying guardrails across platforms. Geographic nuance in threat intelligence and clear RACI ownership are stressed to close gaps between silos.

The conversation closes on trust in automated decisions: transparency, ethics, and privacy ideals, with a human decision-maker retaining final accountability as AI accelerates delivery. Mature organizations are described as elevating cyber literacy at the board and sometimes promoting security executives into broader leadership—while insisting that skilled staff and sustained evaluation of the threat surface remain non-negotiable.

talks.title: Resilience In The Age Of Unknowns The Cxo Playbook Forward1
talks.teaser: Manufacturing, defense, and OT leaders explain how cyber resilience must combine technology, business continuity, and supply-chain control.
talks.summary:
The discussion opens by framing resilience as more than backups, compliance checklists, and familiar metrics. Panelists tie their answers to AI-driven attacks, tangled supply chains, and unstable geopolitics, arguing that leaders need plans for unknown threats rather than only replaying past incidents.

A manufacturing CISO describes plants where physical safety and uptime dominate, robotics and IoT expand the production attack surface, and IT–OT links must contain internal and external threats. India’s defense cyber director characterizes adversaries as well-resourced nation-states, outlines assume-breach thinking, zero-trust limits on lateral movement, and coordinated intelligence with civil and private inputs. He notes static, signature-style defenses lag AI-enabled attackers and points to Ukraine’s shift toward manual operations as one resilience pattern.

Another panelist stresses that resilience spans prediction, endurance, and recovery, and that operations can still fail when technology does. A 2021 U.S. oil and gas disruption illustrates over-reliance on digital controls; manual, disconnected, or business-defined workarounds matter when systems are down. The manufacturing voice details vendor laptops on plant floors, secure remote access, TPRM-style supplier requirements, and periodic third-party assessments. Closing themes cover decades-long platforms versus fast-moving threats: modular designs, protecting long-lived data, skepticism about one-size Western crypto mandates, quantum timeline pressures, and the tradeoffs of linking legacy OT to analytics-heavy IT.

talks.title: Visibility, Mitigation And Governance For Your Exploding Ai Attack Surface
talks.teaser: Practitioners learn how to inventory shadow AI, close exposure gaps, and govern enterprise agents amid rapid generative AI adoption.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames artificial intelligence as the newest expansion of enterprise attack surface, building on familiar exposure-management ideas: organizations cannot protect what they cannot see. Citing rapid business adoption, the speaker notes generative AI use grew about 3.2× in 2025 compared with 2024, with a majority of enterprises deploying AI for business benefit, heavy reliance on third-party packages, and roughly one fifth of AI services holding broad access to corporate data with little auditing.

Practical risk questions follow: how many copilots, studios, chat tools, or agents run internally, whether data exfiltration through AI is visible, and whether AI-targeted attacks are understood. Shadow AI driven by business units, unsanctioned tools, browser extensions, and agents wired to sensitive HR or marketing data illustrate hidden paths when guardrails fail. The middle of the talk maps a strategy—discover inventory first, then define sanctioned versus unsanctioned use, policies, and boundaries, and continuously watch authorized apps for jailbreaks, prompt injection, and risky connections.

Product capabilities described include scanner-based AI discovery branded as AI aware, AI SPM for custom LLM builds, and a broader AI exposure offering positioned as context beyond pattern-matching DLP, proxy, or CASB controls. Analyst quadrant mentions reinforce exposure management as one program spanning cloud, identity, and AI. The close invites deeper discussion at a booth workshop on identity and AI exposure.

talks.title: #NullconBerlin2025 | Derandomizing Kernel Object Locations w Software Hardware-Induced Side Channels
talks.teaser: Research shows software and hardware timing channels that recover kernel heap object locations for more reliable Linux exploitation.
talks.summary:
Kernel privilege escalation usually chains bugs into overwrite, read, and write primitives to learn where critical objects live before hijacking control flow. Failed steps often crash the machine, inviting forensics that can burn stealth and zero-days. The presentation reframes that problem by leaking addresses through side channels that avoid unstable exploit gymnastics.

The first technique times hash-bucket walks triggered by syscalls such as POSIX timer and futex operations. Occupancy differences expose collisions tied to kernel pointers; an offline search over aligned mmstruct slab placements recovers addresses in under a minute on x86-64, with similar ideas on ARM64 and RISC-V. A live run against current Ubuntu still succeeds. Disclosure to the Linux security team yielded a rejected Keith Cook mitigation described as ineffective.

The second technique uses prefetch-driven TLB timing to distinguish mapped versus unmapped kernel virtual memory and recently touched pages, revealing section bases and—after steering targets onto 4 KiB mappings via vmap regions, certain hardening options, or module load side effects—narrowing pages through overlapping syscall access patterns. Demonstrations recover heap objects, stacks, credentials-related structures, and page tables across several Ubuntu kernels on Intel, AMD, and some ARM cores, including mobile. Practitioners should treat these channels as quiet address primitives that improve exploit reliability, and recognize that performance-oriented kernel changes may not eliminate hardware-level leakage.

talks.title: #NullconBerlin2025 | Finding Bugs in V8: A Formal Verification Approach by Simon Gerst
talks.teaser: Applies bounded model checking to V8's range analysis, turning counterexamples into JavaScript proofs of concept.
talks.summary:
Simon Gerst, a security engineer, presents research he began during his studies on finding bugs in the range analysis of V8, the JavaScript engine used in Chrome. Range analysis estimates the possible values of variables so the optimising compiler can drop code that can never run. Because a wrong result in such an optimisation can lead to security vulnerabilities, the speaker argues it must be proven correct, and floating-point details such as negative zero and NaN make that difficult. He walks through abstract interpretation over ranges and sets, interval arithmetic, and how bounded model checking turns a program into a formula whose counterexamples expose violations.

He then describes a harness that drives V8's abstract operators from C++ using the ESBMC tool, and a pipeline that converts each counterexample into a JavaScript proof of concept. Representing ranges as sets of eight values lets generated code reach awkward floating-point ranges, and splitting or scaling ranges handles cases where distinct values are too sparse. Running the tool on an earlier V8 commit, he found a new bug in the division operator tied to a negative-zero edge case, which the V8 team confirmed; at the time of the talk it was still unpatched. The tool also rediscovered three older range-analysis bugs and several synthetic faults he inserted.

The takeaway is that bounded model checking works well for simple operations and self-contained functions, but complex floating-point logic remains a major challenge. Within the time limits, the less-than and equality operators could be shown correct only for limited ranges, while division and other operators ran into timeouts or tool errors, so full correctness was not proven. The work also led to roughly 2.5k lines of contributions and over 40 pull requests to ESBMC.

talks.title: #NullconBerlin2025 | A Deep Dive into A Vulnerability Apple Deems Unexploitable by Mickey Jin
talks.teaser: Walks through a file-copy race condition in macOS that leads to symlink-following and a TCC bypass.
talks.summary:
The talk examines a time-of-check to time-of-use flaw in the copyfile routine that macOS system APIs use to copy files along with their metadata. The speaker explains why copy calls are risky in privileged processes: the API is meant to refuse following symbolic links, but its implementation checks the source file type and opens the source in separate steps. A narrow gap between those steps lets an attacker swap a regular file for a symlink before the open happens.

The speaker reproduces the race under a debugger, then makes it reliable by forcing the clone path to fail through a cross-volume mount and running a loop that keeps swapping the source between a regular file and a symlink. In theory each attempt succeeds about 25% of the time. Apple's first patch added a check after the open, but the speaker showed the window remained, turning the race into a three-fetch problem and lowering the odds to 12.5%. A later fix verified file identity through the open file descriptor. The speaker then demonstrates the bug in a system service that has full disk access, using it to read a protected messages database.

The takeaways are that narrow race windows should not be underestimated, that added checks do not help unless the window itself is closed, and that privileged code should use descriptor-based file operations. Because an attacker needs only one success, retry loops matter, and the speaker recommends testing vendor patches for bypasses soon after release.

talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in #NullconBerlin2025 | LPEPM - Tricking Microsoft EPM To Do Our Bidding by Philip & Rotem.
talks.summary: Autumn Salenas and Philip Zukerman reverse Microsoft Intune Endpoint Privilege Management, the product meant to let non-admins run approved programs through just-in-time virtual accounts. They show a check-versus-use gap: the service hashes an allowed file, then creates the process later, so a swapped payload inherits elevation. After Microsoft’s patch—exclusive opens, final-path checks, and a driver re-hash—they describe still reaching disallowed code when rules cover scripts or installers, when a UNC path is supplied directly to the service, or when an allowed process has a DLL search-order issue. Microsoft rated the follow-ups moderate and pointed operators at documentation that says hash rules should also pin a path users cannot write.

talks.teaser: Covers LKRG 1.0 runtime integrity checks for the Linux kernel and tasks, attack responses, perf tradeoffs, and encrypted remote logging.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the history of Linux Kernel Runtime Guard, from Adam Zabroski’s founding work and the 2018 public release through Openwall, to CIQ’s push for the 1.0 milestone. Solar Designer frames LKRG as imperfect but useful runtime defense at kernel privilege: integrity checking for kernel code, modules, CPU security settings, and per-task state, plus configurable reactions when tampering is detected.

The middle walks through how the guard snapshots and updates legitimate state—static branches, credential changes, namespaces—and validates tasks at permission checks with lightweight control-flow sanity checks. Version 1.0 adds narrowed performance overhead, remote logging over Noise/TCP, blocking risky usermode-helper abuse, and workarounds for Intel CET and Clang CFI when hooking non-exported kernel symbols. Independent thesis work and field reports on exploits and rootkits illustrate what detections succeed and where bypasses appear when attackers patch LKRG itself.

Practitioners should treat LKRG as one layer among hardening options, not a substitute for patching or upstream KSPP-style work. The talk closes on broad kernel version and architecture support, CI packaging, measured ~2.5% benchmark overhead, and roadmap items such as symbol hiding and stronger namespace-focused hardening.

talks.title: #NullconBerlin2025 | RDP and The Power of Deterministic Snapshot Fuzzing by Pascal Beyer
talks.teaser: Walks through snapshot fuzzing findings in a Windows kernel driver and the RDP client, including a hard-to-reproduce race.
talks.summary:
The talk argues for snapshot fuzzing, where a saved memory and register state of a system is loaded into a deterministic emulator and fed random inputs. The speaker lists what such a setup needs: fast reset to the snapshot, a way to separate real crashes from ordinary exceptions, and coverage collection. He then presents his own tool, which boots Windows under a custom hypervisor, takes snapshots, and lets target-specific code define input injection and crash detection.

The first case is a kernel bug in the Windows AFD driver, reached through a legacy TDX handle exposed by an undocumented IO control code. Fuzzing from a snapshot produced a general protection fault in a reference-counting function, caused by a non-canonical pointer taken from the input, which allows an arbitrary increment. Next, a out-of-bounds read in an RDP client session info packet was found using address-sanitizer-style checks built into the emulator. Extra permission bits mark inaccessible heap bytes, and allocation hooks track heap activity. A mismatch between two structure versions leaked heap metadata during a reconnect.

The most involved case is a remote code execution bug in the RDP dynamic virtual channel manager. A race between closing event handles and an asynchronous channel callback led to a use-after-free that reached a stack variable. Deterministic replay, with access breakpoints on the handle table entry, let the speaker trace who signaled the event. The crash only reproduced reliably once thread priorities lined up, which the speaker traced to foreground window boosts. The takeaway is that deterministic execution makes timing-dependent bugs repeatable and debuggable.

talks.title: Berlin 2024 | EV Charging Stations Security - Free Of Charge
talks.teaser: Stephan Gerling analyzes Berlin 2024 | EV Charging Stations Security - Free Of Charge.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, an industrial control systems (ICS) security researcher explores the security posture of electric vehicle (EV) charging stations and wall boxes. Driven by the exponential growth of the EV market and the industry's rush to ensure user convenience comparable to refueling petrol cars, station manufacturers frequently rely on outdated technologies while neglecting foundational security practices. The speaker analyzes the physical security, internal architecture, network protocols, and authentication mechanisms of EV chargers, demonstrating multiple vulnerabilities that allow attackers to reboot stations, extract sensitive data, and obtain free charging.

### Key Topics
- **EV Charging Infrastructure & Protocols**: Examination of the Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP) architecture, backend communications, and regulatory mandates in Germany (such as requirements for ad hoc charging and card payment terminals).
- **Physical Security Deficiencies**: Weak housing protections, easily bypassed standard cabinet locks, lack of tamper detection, and vulnerable internal components.
- **Authentication Weaknesses**: Reliance solely on RFID/NFC card Unique Identifiers (UIDs) without cryptographic validation, enabling straightforward cloning and authorization spoofing.
- **Network & Service Flaws**: Unauthenticated local web interfaces, exposed administrative functions, information leaks in log files, and remote reboot denial-of-service vulnerabilities.
- **Vendor Response & Responsible Disclosure**: The hurdles encountered during coordinated vulnerability disclosure, culminating in vendors declaring affected products end-of-life rather than issuing fixes.

### Technical Details
- **Physical Access & Hardware Layout**: The speaker demonstrated that charging station cabinets frequently use standard electrical locks easily opened with basic triangular keys or improvised tools, lacking tamper switches or robust seals. Internally, stations feature an Ethernet switch, embedded computer boards, microcontrollers, smart meters, power relays, and often a cellular SIM modem for remote maintenance. Connecting to an unused port on the internal switch allowed direct, unauthenticated local network access without needing hardware debug headers like JTAG or UART.
- **Denial-of-Service via Port 8192**: Running an Nmap scan revealed open ports on the embedded system. Sending a specially crafted packet to port 8192 forced the charging station to reboot. Because stations on the test network were interconnected, this reboot packet could be routed across the backend to remotely crash stations located hundreds of kilometers away. The speaker noted that synchronized reboots across large numbers of high-draw stations could theoretically be combined with other grid-level attacks to threaten grid stability.
- **Unauthenticated Web Server (Port 8888) & Log Extraction**: An unprotected HTTP server was identified running on port 8888. It exposed an administrative interface permitting any connected user to download system log files (including the authorization cache) without authentication. These logs stored authorization IDs in decimal and hexadecimal, along with vehicle telemetry such as Electric Vehicle IDs (EV-IDs), vehicle models (e.g., BMW i3), and remaining battery capacities. This data could facilitate long-term tracking of specific vehicles.
- **Free Charging via UID Spoofing & Whitelisting**: Station access control depended entirely on reading the static UID of NFC/RFID charging cards (e.g., MIFARE Classic). Attackers can obtain valid UIDs from rental cars, brute-force sequential IDs, or extract historical authorized UIDs directly from the exposed station log files. Once extracted, the UID can be emulated using devices like a Chameleon Mini or Flipper Zero, or a new custom UID can be added directly via the station's unauthenticated web-based RFID whitelist. To demonstrate arbitrary power drawing, the speaker connected a test box with a standard AC socket to power a waffle maker.

### Takeaways
The speaker concluded that many deployed EV charging stations are effectively broken by design due to flawed security assumptions—specifically assuming physical enclosures cannot be breached and treating unencrypted, legacy protocols (like OCPP 1.6) as sufficient. When these vulnerabilities were disclosed to the manufacturer, communication stalled after the vendor dismissed their security developer, ultimately leading the vendor to mark the hardware end-of-life to avoid releasing a firmware patch. True security improvements will require mandatory backend encryption, cryptographic card authentication (such as ISO 15118 support in OCPP 2.0.1), and robust physical tamper protections.

talks.title: Goa 2023 | Self-Signed, Why Not! Exploiting Insecure Certificate Validation In iOS And macOS
talks.teaser: Shows how certificate validation flaws in iOS and macOS apps let attackers intercept traffic, and how to find and fix them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how apps on iOS and macOS handle TLS certificate validation, and why a self-signed certificate can still get past clients where checks are switched off. The speaker notes that validation is optional in most TLS libraries and is often disabled by developers chasing quick fixes. A man-in-the-middle position lets an attacker offer such a certificate. To test many validators at once, connections are told apart by details in the TLS client hello, such as the requested server name, ciphers and extensions.

A live demo intercepted an iPhone through a Wi-Fi access point and a laptop acting as a router. A game client accepted the forged certificate and exposed an authorization token in its login traffic. The vendor replied that the issue would not be fixed because abuse would be detected and the account flagged. The App Store accepted the fake certificate and revealed which packages were being downloaded, but package checks blocked tampered files. The built-in Books app accepted a modified ebook. Across all tested products, the speaker counted roughly 100 vulnerable applications on iOS, macOS, Android, Windows, game consoles and IoT devices, with about 50 unfixed at the time.

For testers, the takeaway is to check apps for disabled certificate validation and report what is found, with the speaker reporting over $140,000 in bounties. For developers, the advice is to use the built-in TLS APIs, read their documentation, check hostnames manually in low-level libraries, avoid custom validators, and run unit tests against a deliberately self-signed test host. The speaker also suggests build-time warnings, app store rejection of apps with validation disabled, and safer TLS APIs from platform vendors.

talks.title: Goa 2023 | Jailbreaking The Apple HomePod: Fun With Checkm8 And Smart Speakers
talks.teaser: Shows how a bootrom exploit gives code execution on an Apple HomePod and what a jailbroken speaker can then do.
talks.summary:
The talk covers jailbreaking Apple's HomePod smart speaker, which runs a customized tvOS on an A8 chip vulnerable to the checkm8 bootrom exploit. Earlier efforts, such as a virtualized tvOS build and a community hardware connector, never produced a lasting jailbreak, and the checkra1n tool stopped working around iOS 15. The presenter shows how to open the enclosure with heat and a screwdriver and reach the USB port through a cheap 3D-printed adapter with pogo pins.

The exploit path follows the boot chain. The bootrom exploit remaps a bootrom page into SRAM by editing page tables, patches out signature checks, and boots a patched iBoot. A custom ramdisk loader then mounts the real root filesystem, injects code into launchd, and enables SSH. Launchd is patched so every new process loads a tweak-injection library, allowing hooks into system daemons. Because the sealed system snapshot is restored on a normal reboot, changes disappear, which the speaker notes can protect against bricking.

Demonstrations included a custom timer sound, streaming music from an Android device through a Spotify daemon, rewriting Siri replies, routing Siri queries to a chat model, and using the microphone as a covert listening device. The talk ends by noting that a jailbroken HomePod leaves no persistent indicators, has no microphone light, and can only be re-exploited by rebooting it, so owners should unplug idle devices.

talks.title: Goa 2023 | Cracking With Automated USB Fuzz By Subba Bachina & Conna
talks.teaser: Presents a self-recovering USB fuzzing platform and shows how descriptor-focused mutation speeds finding host-side bugs.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why USB matters as an omnipresent attack surface, then walks through host–device roles, descriptors, and transfer types so listeners can reason about how untrusted peripherals negotiate capabilities with a computer.

The core contribution is USB Studio, positioned as an enhanced successor to the long-used FaceDancer approach. A separate control host drives fuzzing while the hardware mimics keyboards, cameras, and similar classes across Windows, Linux, and Android. The design stresses self-power and automatic recovery after host crashes—called out as a weakness in many interceptors—plus genetic mutation over protocol descriptors, corpus growth, and a feedback path for crash logs to shorten campaigns. Layered firmware, Lua glue, and a GUI round out the architecture.

Practitioners see how built-in UVC support reframes time-consuming manual protocol work from prior Windows Hello camera attacks, and a live demo where fuzzed traffic triggered a Windows blue screen reported to MSRC. The close covers roadmap items such as deeper physical-layer analysis, proxy mode, Wi-Fi linking multiple fuzzers, and richer debugger-fed feedback loops.

talks.title: Goa 2023 | Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) Protection: Challenges & Opportunities
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Goa 2023 | Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) Protection: Challenges & Opportunities.
talks.summary:
### Overview
At Nullcon Goa 2023, leadership from India's National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC) and chief information security officers (CISOs) from key critical sectors convened to discuss the challenges, regulatory landscape, and collaborative opportunities in securing Critical Information Infrastructure (CII). Governed under Sections 70 and 70A of the IT Act, CII encompasses computer resources whose incapacitation would have a debilitating impact on national security, the economy, public health, or safety. The panel focused on bridging the gap between national regulatory bodies, corporate enterprises, and the independent security research community.

### Key Topics
- **Legal & Structural Mandate of NCIIPC:** Defined under the IT Act, NCIIPC identifies critical infrastructure and assesses security baselines across seven designated critical sectors: Banking, Financial Services and Insurance (BFSI); Power & Energy; Telecom; Transport; Health; Strategic and Public Enterprises; and Government. Over 100 organizations have been assessed and notified as protected systems, carrying strict legal deterrence including up to 10 years imprisonment for unauthorized access attempts.
- **Evolving Threat Landscape:** The DG of NCIIPC highlighted a surge in attack sophistication, specifically from Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actors and state-sponsored groups seeking long-term persistence after reconnaissance. Prominent threats include major ransomware incidents (citing disruptions at Oil India Limited, JNPT ports, and pharmaceutical entities such as Sun Pharma and Granules India), managed service provider supply-chain attacks, ransomware-as-a-service, and emerging attack surfaces introduced by rapid cloud migration, AI, and quantum computing.
- **CISO Perspectives on Interdependence & Threat Intel:** Panelists representing major enterprises (ICICI Bank, Vodafone, and the National Stock Exchange) stressed extreme interdependencies. With large enterprises managing tens of thousands of suppliers (up to 40,000+), supply chain vulnerabilities pose severe risks. The CISO of NSE noted that NCIIPC's daily threat intelligence feed demonstrates higher actionable relevance than commercial threat feeds, reporting a 25–30% hit rate in their environment, alongside valuable monitoring of upstream telecom provider edge routers.
- **Auditing Limitations and Continuous Compliance:** A primary discussion centered on CERT-In empaneled audits. The panel acknowledged severe constraints: a shortage of auditors (only around 150 empaneled firms), inconsistent audit quality, and the inherent limitation that standard compliance audits represent a point-in-time check rather than real-time security posture. Moving toward continuous compliance and API-driven telemetry was advocated.

### Technical Details
- **Collaborative Log & Telemetry Analysis:** Critical entities share ingress and egress logs directly with NCIIPC, providing a secondary layer of correlation and visibility above internal Security Operations Centers (SOCs).
- **Telemetry Standardization:** Speakers discussed open standardization efforts, such as the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework (OCSF) supported by 60+ security vendors, to correlate alerts across the 40 to 50 disparate tools typical within an enterprise environment.
- **Crowdsourced Security and Red Teaming:** NCIIPC announced an upcoming institutional crowdsourcing initiative to connect vetted ethical hackers and vulnerability researchers with willing CII entities. Testing will be performed in controlled environments, with recognition and reward structures proportional to vulnerability severity.

### Takeaways
Securing national infrastructure requires moving beyond mere paper compliance and point-in-time checklists toward continuous monitoring, red-team penetration testing, and tactical peer-to-peer threat sharing. NCIIPC emphasized its commitment to collaborating directly with independent researchers, ethical hackers, and academic institutions to uncover and remediate critical vulnerabilities before adversaries exploit them.

talks.title: Goa 2023 | Unlocking Any Door In 21st Century. Immersion In Bio-Security - Timur; Aleksandra
talks.teaser: Shows how three face-recognition and doorbell devices bought in Europe were bypassed, from sensor tricks to weak crypto.
talks.summary:
The speakers examined facial recognition used for door access and employee time tracking, walking through a typical pipeline that detects, aligns, extracts features and matches against a threshold. They bought three devices sold for the European market: an access terminal, an infrared-only time clock and a Wi-Fi smart doorbell with cloud storage.

On the access terminal, the depth camera was not used in the decision, so a sheet of glass between the cameras and a photo shown to the visible camera could get past the check. The terminal also preferred the larger face in frame. A remote code execution flaw let them extract models, and they generated a synthetic face with a variational autoencoder and a super-resolution network, tuned toward the 2,500 score threshold. The time clock relied on Gabor and local binary pattern features and was thrown off by glasses, while a printed film lit by infrared light mimicked depth. The doorbell sent traffic without certificate pinning, used weakly signed firmware, derived its storage key from a weak generator and the clock, had a path traversal in its cloud signing, and exposed a USB debug shell.

The lessons were that added technology enlarges the attack surface, newer machine learning is not automatically more robust, and cheap devices often miss basic controls. Vendor responses were slow and vague, so the speakers offered their slides and a biometric security checklist instead of a published white paper.

talks.title: Goa 2023 | Reverse Engineering RGB Keyboard Backlights With Linux Kernel Drivers by Rishit
talks.teaser: Shows how reverse engineering a closed Windows app led to a Linux kernel driver controlling HP laptop keyboard backlight zones.
talks.summary:
The talk follows a hobby project to reverse engineer the RGB keyboard backlight control on an HP laptop and reimplement it as a Linux kernel driver. The backlight is driven by a closed-source Windows application with no documentation. The speaker began by locating its background service, then recognised a .NET binary and used a decompiler on it, which still held readable names, to find one routine that passed operation codes into a WMI management object.

ACPI bytecode is stored in firmware and loaded into memory at boot, while WMI routes requests from user space to ACPI methods through a GUID and a special ACPI device entry. Dumping the ACPI tables and parsing the mapping bytes exposed the method that controls the backlight. The kernel's ACPI support offers a WMI evaluate call, which the speaker wrapped in a driver exposing an LED device with brightness and per-zone files in sysfs. Windows offered only on and off, so brightness was emulated by scaling zone colour values.

A live demo showed the driver switching the light on and off, writing colours to zones, and running a fast pattern script. The talk ended with upstream work: an initial contribution to the mainline 6.x kernel and ongoing HP WMI changes with maintainers, aiming for a shared standard for keyboard RGB control on Linux. The main takeaway is that vendor-specific features can be recovered by reading closed binaries and firmware-defined interfaces, then reproduced through standard kernel APIs.

talks.title: Goa 2023 | Android-SigMorph: Covert Communication Exploiting Android Signing Schemes
talks.teaser: Explains how extra data can ride in Android APK signing blocks while signatures still verify, and why that matters.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how Android APK files are signed and where the signing format leaves room for extra data that does not break a valid signature. The presenters start with the Android signing schemes, describing V1 as built on JAR signing, where only files listed in META-INF are covered. They also recap older V1 weaknesses, such as unprotected extra files and duplicate classes.dex entries.

The core of the session is the V2 scheme and the APK signing block placed before the central directory. The speakers explain which parts are covered by the digest and which are not. Optional blocks such as verity padding, source stamp, Google Play frosting, dependency info and channel blocks are examined one by one. They show that editing the verity padding in a signed Facebook APK still passed verification. They also note that the central directory offset is unprotected, which lets large amounts of data be added. A survey found around 51% of the malware samples used only V1 signing. In a demo, a dormant app read a payload from a fixed offset in an installed APK.

The talk closes with V4, which signs the whole file separately, and with apksigner crashes caused by oversized block sizes. The takeaways are that attackers can use the signing block to hide payloads, and that defenders should not treat a signature check or a verifier's pass as proof that an APK is clean.

talks.title: Goa 2023 | How I Hacked Your Bank Account: A Detailed Look At UPI Security by Nemo
talks.teaser: Shows how a UPI banking app skipped SMS verification of a phone number, letting an attacker sign up as someone else.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how UPI, India's instant mobile payment system, links phone numbers to bank accounts and why its bank-transfer design makes payments hard to reverse. The speaker splits the system into the app, the UPI backend, the shared NPCI library and the bank's core ledger, and shows that a user's phone number is stored in three places that must agree. Trust is extended to the backend's internal requests, so lookups such as bank account discovery need no authentication once a request comes from inside that trusted side.

The main case is an Android app from a smaller bank. During first-time setup, the app sent the phone number and date of birth to the backend, which issued a token and waited for an SMS from the device. The backend never compared the sender's number with the number on the profile it had created. By skipping steps in the app, the speaker registered a profile under another person's number without sending any message. For new users this exposed bank account numbers, and for existing users it also gave access to transaction history. Withdrawing money still required the PIN, and the speaker noted that four-digit PINs and inconsistent rate limits make guessing feasible at scale.

The speaker argues the flaw was missed because heavy obfuscation, SSL pinning and field-level encryption slowed down testers, who often work to tight deadlines. The suggested fixes are open security standards for UPI, pentests on builds with the protections removed, and a vulnerability disclosure program that spans banks rather than only individual payment companies.

talks.title: Berlin 2023 | Security Journey In French Network Access Controller by Baptiste David
talks.teaser: Shows how an open-source captive portal's login crypto, admin panel and missing CSRF checks chain into root access.
talks.summary:
Captive portals sit in front of a network's internet gateway and make users authenticate before traffic is allowed out, which also lets operators record who connected. This talk looks at Alcazar, an open-source network access controller, and examines how its login and administration components were built. The speaker explains that the default setup served the login over plain HTTP, so passwords crossed the network unprotected.

The speaker then walks through a home-made password obfuscation scheme that combined a challenge value, an MD5 hash with a shared secret and an XOR step. Because the output was truncated to the password's length, the password length leaked and partial collisions became practical. A later move to SHA-256 kept the same truncation flaw, and the administrator notification mechanism used MD5 by default, so intercepted traffic could be cracked. Separately, the admin panel passed user-controlled values into shell commands after stripping quotes instead of escaping them, and its pages lacked anti-CSRF tokens.

In a live demo, a crafted link opened by a logged-in administrator triggered the flawed command path and produced a reverse shell with root privileges. The takeaways are to keep captive portals on HTTPS with proper certificates, avoid custom cryptography, use strong secrets, add CSRF protection to administrative interfaces, and treat portal admin access as high-value. The speaker withheld some specifics until the project ships a fix.

talks.title: Berlin 2023 | The Invasion Of Bad Drivers by Omer Tsarfati
talks.teaser: Examines risky Windows kernel drivers in gaming tools, IOCTL pitfalls, WinIO abuse, and a Razer plugin race for SYSTEM.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why consumer gaming hardware ships kernel-mode software, then walks through how Windows exposes drivers via device objects, symbolic links, and IOCTL dispatch routines. It explains how transfer methods such as METHOD_NEITHER, buffered, and direct I/O shape memory handling, and how missing probes, weak length checks, and mishandled IRP fields routinely yield crashes, information leaks, or arbitrary kernel writes.

The middle ties those patterns to real products. Analysis of MSI-related WinIO code shows a stack overflow without stack protection, plus port I/O and physical memory mapping reachable from less privileged contexts. A parallel look at Razer Synapse’s WinRing0 driver highlights MSR read and write primitives and a mismatch between permissive driver logic and a later locked-down security descriptor. The speaker describes winning a load-time race by triggering a low-privilege plugin install so the device stays open long enough to overwrite the syscall MSR and escalate to SYSTEM.

The close covers scaling discovery: similar debug strings on VirusTotal surfaced 114 related drivers reused across many vendors. Enabling Hyper-V blocks some MSR tampering but leaves other issues. Practitioners are urged to avoid WinIO-style code bases, harden IOCTL handling, and combine hypervisor and anti-malware controls where end users cannot remove the underlying drivers.

talks.title: Berlin 2023 | The Achilles Heel Of The macOS Gatekeeper by Jonathan Bar Or
talks.teaser: Explains a Gatekeeper bypass that abuses AppleDouble metadata and restrictive ACLs so downloaded apps skip quarantine checks.
talks.summary:
This talk, given by a Microsoft Defender research architect, examines how macOS Gatekeeper decides whether a downloaded app may run. Browsers tag downloads with the com.apple.quarantine extended attribute, and Gatekeeper uses that tag together with code signing and notarization when the file is first opened. The speaker sets a narrow definition of a bypass: it must not start from existing code execution or an unsupported file system.

The talk reviews earlier Gatekeeper bypasses in two groups. One group stops the quarantine attribute from being written, such as a path longer than 886 characters. The other lets the attribute be written but fails to enforce policy afterwards. Searching for new cases, the speaker read the open-source file copying code and found that AppleDouble metadata files inside archives are parsed and applied, including a special ACL text attribute. Black-box fuzzing and attempts to forge the quarantine flag produced little, since Safari overwrote the flag.

The working exploit was a zip archive holding an app and an AppleDouble file with a restrictive ACL. When Archive Utility extracted it, the ACL blocked the later quarantine write, so the app opened with no prompt. The demo ran with Lockdown Mode enabled. Apple fixed the issue in a later macOS release after disclosure in July 2022. For defenders, the talk suggests hunting for restrictive ACLs in AppleDouble files inside archives, extracted content missing the quarantine flag, and apps that do not run from app translocation. It also stresses that Lockdown Mode does not replace keeping macOS updated.

talks.teaser: Covers abusing C++ stack unwinding after overflows, from failed CTF releases to multi-OS exploits and academic publication.

The presenters frame their work as a multi-course story rather than a straight technical brief. It begins with a fictional code review: a signed-length stack copy that normally dies on overflow, except a custom segmentation-fault handler throws into C++-style exception machinery with jump buffers sitting on the attacker-influenced stack. That corner case becomes a Capture The Flag challenge they could not ship without a working exploit, which forces a deeper look at how libstdc++ unwinding walks frames after canary failure.

They generalize the idea into confusion primitives and gadget outcomes—forward and backward control-flow hijacks, arbitrary read/write, and free primitives—and test mitigations such as stack canaries, shadow stacks, and Intel CET on Linux, Android, Windows, iOS, and macOS. Debian package analysis and Binary Ninja taint tracking quantify how often useful gadgets appear. Real proofs follow, including CVE-2009-4009 and later bugs in LibreOffice and macOS smart-card login code, woven into a top-tier academic submission, revision, and acceptance arc.

Vendor reactions range from silence to moderate severity acknowledgments and compiler-side mitigations. Community pushback highlights earlier related CTF write-ups without the same control-flow diversion. Practitioners hear that once a stack overflow exists, unwinding may keep using attacker-corrupted state despite canaries, and that CTF rabbit holes can mature into systematic, publishable vulnerability research.

talks.title: Berlin 2023 | (In)Secure Remote Operations: What Sucks, Rocks, And A Super-CLI by Yossi
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Berlin 2023 | (In)Secure Remote Operations: What Sucks, Rocks, And A Super-CLI by Yossi.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, speaker Yossi—co-founder of 10Root Cybersecurity and former co-founder of Javelin Networks—explores the mechanisms of remote administration and lateral movement across Microsoft Windows environments. The talk frames remote administration tools and attack techniques as sharing the exact same underlying APIs and protocols, emphasizing that context differentiates an administrator's task from an adversary's activity. Yossi advocates for a CLI-centric, "living off the land" philosophy for both red teams and blue teams, contrasting traditional tools like RDP, RPC, and PsExec with PowerShell Remoting (WinRM/WS-Man), detailing credential exposure realities, and demonstrating built-in Active Directory defenses.

### Key Topics
- **Living off the Land:** Leveraging native operating system binaries (LOLBins), APIs, and system services (RPC, DCOM, WMI, SMB) to conduct administration or lateral movement without relying on external malware.
- **Pre-Authentication & Port Analysis:** How tools establish connections prior to full authentication, observed via an object-based `netstat` loop (`Get-NetTCPConnection`).
- **Inter-Process and Inter-Box Communication via Named Pipes:** Utilizing SMB (port 445) named pipes to construct stealthy, firewall-friendly reverse shells and C2 channels.
- **RDP Attacks and Insecurities:** Exploiting RDP using man-in-the-middle scripts to downgrade encryption to RC4, abuse CredSSP, spoof self-signed certificates, extract NetNTLM hashes, and capture cleartext credentials when Network Level Authentication (NLA) is disabled.
- **PowerShell Remoting (WinRM):** Operational advantages of WS-Management (single-port, encrypted HTTP/HTTPS traffic, background job execution, and session-based file transfer without SMB) alongside Just Enough Administration (JEA) session configurations.
- **Credential Exposure & Token Duplication:** Challenging Microsoft documentation regarding remote logon types by duplicating primary process tokens from `wsmprovhost.exe` to achieve network authentication, along with using virtual accounts (`RunAsVirtualAccount`) to mitigate exposure.
- **Preventing Lateral Movement with Native AD Controls:** Restricting privileged accounts using Active Directory's `logonWorkstations` attribute to block pass-the-hash, LDAP binds, and remote invocation without commercial software.

### Technical Details
- **RPC Subsystem Dependencies:** Yossi demonstrates that over 200 system services depend on the Microsoft RPC subsystem service on modern Windows machines, making it impossible to harden an OS simply by shutting down RPC.
- **Named Pipe C2:** Named pipe server and client streams can ride on port 445 (SMB) and pipe commands directly into `Invoke-Expression` (`IEX`), bypassing firewall restrictions and avoiding process-binding alerts.
- **Fixing Clock Skew Remotely:** If Kerberos fails due to a clock discrepancy greater than five minutes, an administrator or attacker can invoke WinRM targeting an IP address (falling back to NTLM) using `$using:localTime` to remotely reset the destination clock.
- **Token Duplication vs. Virtual Accounts:** While tools like Mimikatz show no Kerberos tickets or cached credentials inside LSASS during a Type 3 WinRM session, an attacker with local administrator access can duplicate the primary token from `wsmprovhost.exe` using `Invoke-TokenManipulation` or `KernelCactus`. Enabling `RunAsVirtualAccount = $true` forces the session into a local-only virtual account, causing outgoing Kerberos tickets to bind to the machine account rather than a user domain identity.
- **Logon Workstations Hardening:** Configuring Active Directory user workstation restrictions restricts where authentication requests can originate. Attempts to use pass-the-hash, WMI, PsExec, WinRM, or LDAP queries from unauthorized systems immediately fail across interactive and non-interactive sessions.

### Takeaways
Defenders and red teamers must understand the low-level behavior of native protocols rather than relying strictly on tool marketing or official documentation. PowerShell Remoting and JEA offer powerful, auditable alternatives to swiss-cheese firewall policies created by legacy RPC and RDP services, but default PowerShell configurations require explicit hardening. Finally, simple built-in Active Directory controls like workstation logon limitations can effectively neutralize entire classes of lateral movement without the cost of complex third-party security software.

talks.title: Berlin 2023 | Not So Famous Attack Vectors In The World Of Smart Contract Security!
talks.teaser: Walks through lesser-known smart contract attack vectors, from calldata tricks and gas griefing to metamorphic contracts.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys smart contract attack vectors that get less attention than reentrancy or price manipulation. It starts with call data: when a function takes a narrow parameter such as an 8-bit unsigned integer, extra high-order bits can be appended, and compilers before 0.8 do not check them when raw assembly reads the input. Call data can also be reshaped so a hash-based replay check sees a different value while the function logic still accepts it.

Gas-related issues follow. Since a sub-call gets only about 63/64 of the remaining gas, an attacker can size the gas so an inner call fails silently while the outer transaction succeeds, letting a protocol hand out shares without collecting tokens. A denial-of-service variant abuses return data copying, which is charged to the caller, to exhaust gas. A view function that reads remaining gas can return different values within one transaction, so results should be cached. Metamorphic contracts use CREATE2 and SELFDESTRUCT to redeploy different code at the same address. Web2 issues show that unsanitized on-chain strings or token URIs rendered in a front end allow HTML or script injection. A reverting static call can also leave stale memory that later logic trusts.

The takeaways are to avoid raw assembly or validate its inputs strictly, cache view-call results, check the success of every external call, and sanitize stored data before rendering it.

talks.title: Berlin 2023 | Why I Write My Own Security Tooling & Why You Should Too! by James Forshaw
talks.teaser: Makes the case for writing small, domain-specific research tools, with Windows examples like .NET serialization and COM hunting.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security researchers should write their own domain-specific tooling instead of relying only on general-purpose disassemblers and debuggers. The speaker separates such tools from products like IDA Pro and WinDbg, and suggests starting small with simple automation. One early example is a short IDA Python script that reads the 16-byte GUID at the cursor and formats it as a string, saving repeated manual copying.

Tooling also supports finding vulnerabilities. In older .NET serialization research, a short reflection-based program listed serializable types that implemented an interface executing logic during deserialization, narrowing tens of thousands of classes to a few hundred. Years later the same code gained a check for serializable delegates, which exposed a comparer class in .NET 4.5 that could run code during deserialization. For Windows COM, a browser built to correlate registry data led to a cross-session activation issue that did not require administrator rights. The vendor patched only the reported class, and a second class remained exploitable.

Other benefits include remembering undocumented API behaviour, such as an enumeration call that only worked after opening a specific file name noted in code, and building a Kerberos library to understand the protocol, which revealed bugs. Sharing tools helps others, but antivirus engines often flag analysis code: one compiled tool was detected by 43 of 65 engines on VirusTotal. The takeaways are to start small, write maintainable code, and publish results where useful.

talks.title: Berlin 2023 | SCCI: The Road To Side-Channel Regression Testing In CI Development by Witold
talks.teaser: Shows how to bake side-channel power analysis tests into CI pipelines so timing and power leaks are caught as code changes.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that side-channel leakage, such as power consumption and timing, should be tested continuously in CI/CD pipelines rather than found in a late security review. The speaker, who leads a small embedded security team, described how IoT devices often run off-the-shelf AES on chips without secure elements. In a live demo, a power analysis attack recovered an AES key from a software implementation on an STM32 target after about 500 traces, and a more adaptive approach needed around 20 to 40 traces.

The middle of the talk covered a test-driven workflow in which side-channel tests are written before the code is finished, since they are expected to fail once leaky code appears. Security specialists set up scopes, glitch searches and instrumentation early, while developers keep general regression tests for everyday issues. Attacks are kept broad rather than exploit-focused, and the lab runs on a Linux host with PCI Express passthrough, driven by GitHub Actions and a self-hosted runner. Hardware problems were common, including USB hubs that lack the power-switching circuitry and a shared scope multiplexed with a cheap electromechanical switch.

A constant-time example showed how a password comparison leaked timing after a variable changed from 32-bit to 64-bit, which turned a conditional move into a branch on Arm. A live pipeline run flagged the vulnerable version with failing tests, including one that used only power traces. The speaker closed with masking and per-iteration frequency changes as countermeasures, which make attacks harder rather than impossible.

talks.title: Berlin 2023 | Server Side Prototype Pollution: Blackbox Detection Without The DoS by Gareth
talks.teaser: Shows black-box ways to detect server-side prototype pollution using probes that change behaviour without crashing the server.
talks.summary:
Gareth Hayes opens with the core problem: confirming server-side prototype pollution usually means changing object prototypes on the server, which can easily cause denial of service. He explains how inherited properties and recursive merge functions let attacker-controlled JSON reach the prototype, and notes that remote code execution has been reached through the same flaw in earlier public research.

He then walks through his own attempts. Early probes crashed Node services, so he moved to gentler checks. Changing the allowed parameter count, Express query parsing options, JSON response spacing, CORS exposed headers, a response status code, and removing the HEAD method each produced a visible change that could be reversed. He also described a lodash merge check that drops a probe key when the prototype already holds it, and a SuperJSON check that separates object assignments from primitive ones. For automated testing, he used a Node inspect flag that triggers a DNS lookup to an out-of-band collaborator, with double quotes used to hide the host. Reading inherited property names in cookies and parameters exposed JavaScript engine details on some sites.

He closed by releasing an open-source Burp scanner that implements these techniques, and said that black-box exploitation proved much harder than detection. For prevention he recommended Map and Set instead of plain objects, null-prototype objects, and disabling the proto property in Node, while noting that the flag is only defence in depth.

talks.title: Hacking Fintech Crime Realities & Possibilities by Anand.V & Chander Mohan | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: A research-backed view of India's fintech fraud stack, scam playbooks, and why recovery and policing rarely keep pace.
talks.summary:
The session opens on a Deep Strat study with law enforcement data from Haryana, where fewer than half a percent of cyber fraud complaints became formal investigations. The speaker frames fintech crime as identity fraud first: circular identity graphs, long-lived forged personas, and supply-chain abuse such as fingerprint alteration, photo swaps on KYC updates, and forged biometrics at commercial cost.

The middle maps a "fraud stack" with a core layer of telecom, banking, SIM caches, and mule accounts beneath operational scams. Victim psychology centers on urgency, fear, and greed via "nasty" and "friendly" bank-official scripts that overwhelmingly push OTP sharing or malicious links. Unit economics, agile-style targeting, enumeration against bank portals, SIM takeover, fingerprint lifting from public deeds, and export-license arbitrage illustrate how profits fund growing sophistication.

The close stresses asymmetric scale: split-payment routing, jurisdictional friction, weak FIR conversion, and industrialized tradecraft outpacing fragmented corporate views. Practitioners are urged to reject denial, pursue collective intelligence, shared standards, better analytics, and stronger support for investigators rather than purely product-side fixes.
