talks.title: Unearthing Malicious And Risky OpenSource Packages Using Packj by Ashish Bijlani Devdutt Patnaik
talks.teaser: Explains package registry attacks like typosquatting and hijacked maintainer accounts, and how a vetting tool flags risky packages.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the scale of open-source package managers such as npm, PyPI and RubyGems, where publishing takes minutes and vetting is limited. A typical application pulls in hundreds of transitive dependencies, which makes manual review impractical. The speakers cover the attack routes that follow from this: typosquatting, dependency confusion, social engineering of maintainers, and account takeover through expired email domains.

They walk through real cases. One dependency confusion attack used a higher-versioned public package to displace an internal one. A typosquatted package copied the description of a legitimate project. A recent PyPI package had an expired maintainer email domain that was bought for five dollars, which allowed a password reset and a malicious release that targeted cloud credentials. They also describe the colors and faker sabotage by their own maintainer, where an infinite loop broke many applications, and star-jacking, where a package borrows a popular repository's stars. Known-vulnerability scanners miss such cases because no CVE exists.

The speakers then present Packj, a command-line vetting tool with a cloud service. It checks metadata such as abandonment, maintainer email validity and repository provenance, runs static analysis for file, network and process APIs, and compares runtime behaviour across versions and platforms. In the demo, a popular but abandoned npm package and an old requests release with two known CVEs still drawing heavy downloads were examined. The team reported about 40 malicious PyPI packages, which were then removed.

talks.title: Pushing Security Left By Mutating Byte Code by Gaurav Gogia | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Shows a bytecode language and compiler that encrypt instructions at compile time and runtime to resist reverse engineering.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Mutant, a high-level programming language and compiler meant to move software protection earlier in development. The speaker argues that teams guarding valuable products such as games or security tools currently add obfuscation, encryption and hand-written assembly themselves, which takes time away from features. Mutant compiles source into bytecode that runs on a Mutant virtual machine, or into a self-contained release binary for other platforms, with cross compilation from Windows to Linux, Android-oriented ARM and Mac targets shown live.

The demonstration covered several protections. Bytecode carries a header, a footer and an integrity hash, so a tampered file is rejected. Constants are encrypted at compile time, and individual instructions are decrypted only while they execute and encrypted again afterward. To test this, the speaker compiled a program with a hard-coded credential, captured the memory of a running Mutant binary and of an equivalent C++ program, and searched both dumps for the string. The secret appeared in the C++ dump but not in the Mutant one.

The speaker acknowledged limitations: the key generation is deterministic and open source, the binaries are roughly 30 MB, the project has had little real-world testing, and secure disk and network operations are not yet supported. Planned work includes bytecode compression, more dynamic constants and plugins for LLVM, the JVM or CLR. In the Q&A the speaker called it an academic proof of concept and compared it with existing virtualization-based protectors.

talks.title: Honey I Just Put The Hospital On A Ventilator by Shyam Sundar Ramaswami & Rakesh Mahanthi
talks.teaser: Explores how malicious executables hide inside medical DICOM images and how entropy-based scanning blocks them.
talks.summary:
Hospital imaging has shifted from printed films to DICOM studies moved over PACS and opened in desktop viewers. The speakers outline how the standard’s empty 128-byte preamble and vendor-private tags let a file satisfy a DICOM reader while still behaving as a portable executable.

A from-scratch Python tool splices DOS headers into the preamble, parks the rest of the PE in a private tag, and retargets header pointers so the artifact executes on demand yet still displays as legitimate imaging in tools such as RadiAnt. Upload checks often classify it as both image and executable. The second half sketches follow-on abuse: antivirus and sandbox blind spots, command-and-control callbacks, injection into privileged Windows viewers (sometimes dated installs), optional PowerShell payloads, and harder paths on Linux. Delivery scenarios include email attachments to clinicians, insider access to PACS, cloud endpoints, and poisoned open training datasets.

On defense, GE Healthcare describes static checks tuned for multi-gigabyte objects: Shannon entropy on the preamble, YARA patterns for embedded markup or shell fragments, plus quick, aggressive, and staged scan modes. They note gaps—unrestricted public tags, script in names, preamble space for short commands, and protocols that may omit preamble on device transfers while web-oriented PACS paths carry it—and urge reader vendors to inspect preamble bytes.

talks.title: Hacking Android Foreground Services Escalation Of Privileges by Rony Das | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how Android foreground service timing can be abused to record the microphone without a visible notification.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Nullcon Goa 2022, Rony Das demonstrates a privilege escalation bypass affecting Android foreground services. Das explores how background execution limits introduced in Android 8 (Oreo) mandate sticky foreground notifications whenever applications access sensitive hardware components like the microphone, camera, or GPS. While prior bypasses (notably patched under CVE-2019-2219) attempted to briefly initiate services and stop notifications, Das demonstrates a new threading technique that offloads media recording calls to a separate thread, enabling continuous covert audio recording up to Android 10 without leaving a persistent user notification.

### Key Topics
- **Android Foreground Service Limits**: Android 8 Oreo introduced restrictions preventing background applications from accessing sensitive hardware sensors (microphone, camera, GPS) without an active, non-dismissible foreground notification.
- **The 5-Second Window**: Once `startForegroundService()` is invoked, developers have a strict 5-second window to post a foreground notification, otherwise the Android operating system kills the service.
- **Historical Vulnerability (CVE-2019-2219)**: An earlier technique allowed apps to start a foreground service, hand off audio recording to the Android Media API, and stop the notification. Google addressed this issue with a December 2019 patch.
- **Threading Bypass**: Das discovered that by dispatching audio capture to a background `Runnable`/thread, the main thread can invoke `stopForeground()` almost immediately (within 2–3 seconds), avoiding the persistent sticky notification while audio recording continues unobtrusively.

### Technical Details
In Android's security model, hardware sensors are governed by strict application context and service restrictions. Long-running background spyware needs persistence without visual indicators. Under the documented architecture, calling Android's built-in `Android Media API` delegates recording tasks to Android's media server context, which writes output directly to internal cache storage without requiring custom low-level sensor implementation.

Under CVE-2019-2219, Google patched direct sequential calls because completing the operation inline took too long or failed under updated OS checks. In Das's updated zero-day technique:
1. The malicious service invokes `startForegroundService()`.
2. Immediately, execution dispatches a new thread (`Runnable`) tasked with calling `startRecording()` via the Android Media API for a prolonged duration (e.g., 2 minutes).
3. Because the recording logic runs asynchronously on another thread, the main execution thread immediately calls the stop foreground notification method well within the 5-second deadline (typically within 2 to 3 seconds).
4. The foreground notification disappears almost instantaneously, yet the underlying media server continues recording audio into the application's cache directory.

During a live demo on a physical Android 10 device, Das compared the patched technique against the new threading approach. The demonstration verified that despite no visible notification appearing in the status bar, newly written audio files continuously grew in size within the app's cache directory.

### Takeaways
Das noted that Google resolved the underlying issue in Android 11. However, for Android 10, Google indicated they would not backport a fix due to extensive infrastructure changes required in the operating system. Because Android 10 remained unpatched for this specific flaw, no CVE was assigned for this variant.

talks.title: Jailbreaking iOS In The PostApocalyptic Era by CoolStar Tihmstar | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Walks through post-exploitation steps for iOS jailbreaking, from kernel memory access to sandbox escape and code signing bypasses.
talks.summary:
The talk picks up after an initial kernel exploit has already been obtained and focuses on post-exploitation for iOS jailbreaking. The goals are a stable kernel read and write primitive that survives across processes and reboots, escaping the sandbox to become root, bypassing code signing enforcement, and enabling system-wide code injection for tweaks. It traces how kernel memory access has changed, from simply patching the kernel before iOS 9, through kernel patch protection, to the hardware-enforced KTRR on newer devices.

The middle section walks through the workarounds for each mitigation era. Task ports to the kernel were reused through host special ports, and remapped memory got past pointer checks, while later zone separation was sidestepped with a fake task structure. From iOS 14 onward, a library built on IOSurface connect methods provides the primitive, which is handed between processes and held by launchd. Escaping the sandbox and gaining root involves swapping credential label pointers and adjusting UIDs. Code signing bypasses rely on trust caches, MobileFileIntegrity and CoreTrust, while newer devices need debugger-based tricks and user-space reboots to get code loaded into launchd.

The closing part covers the root filesystem. Remounting it read-write was possible by clearing flags on the root vnode through iOS 14, but sealed snapshots in iOS 15 block that, so files are placed on the data volume instead. The speaker concludes that each new mitigation makes jailbreaking harder, and that arbitrary kernel read and write alone is no longer enough without bypasses for pointer authentication or the page protection layer.

talks.title: CXO Panel: Securing The Software | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Panelists offer practical advice on secure development, from threat modeling and CI/CD scanning to supply chain integrity.
talks.summary:
A panel at Nullcon Goa 2022 discussed how to secure software across the development life cycle. Panelists argued that security and software cannot be separated, and that threat modeling, secure coding rules and scanning tools should apply from design through deployment. They advised customizing tools to cut false positives instead of relying on defaults.

Practical controls came next. Speakers recommended tight privileged access, continuous analysis in CI/CD pipelines, and generating input validation from API specifications so reviewers check one source. For cloud, they pointed to account governance, misconfiguration as a frequent flaw, least-privilege identity policies and avoiding embedded secrets. For build integrity, they proposed zero trust principles, audit trails, and signed build provenance, referencing the OpenSSF and SLSA framework. After the Log4j episode, one speaker suggested adding security to DevOps early, starting with a dependency dashboard for legacy projects before adding preventive gates.

The closing segment covered accountability, with leaders signing off on releases, plain-language minimum requirements, security awareness, defense in depth and attack surface reduction. An audience question about unmaintained open source components led to advice to vet third-party components before they enter a codebase, and to replace or internalise them when they cannot be maintained.

talks.title: Automate Your Whatsapp Chats by Aditi Bhatnagar | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how Android accessibility services can automate WhatsApp chats and why that same power fuels banking trojans and spyware.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with everyday reasons people might want automated replies, then describes a personal experiment that became a competition to flood a friend with notifications. Frustrated with web clients, she wanted something that ran on her Android phone and identified three needs: read the screen, type in the compose field, and tap send.

She walks through Android’s accessibility framework, inspired by TalkBack, and the three setup steps: implement an accessibility service class, declare it in the manifest, and configure package names and event types in XML. Using UI Automator, she maps WhatsApp resource IDs for the contact name, message field, and send button, then demos a small app that sends a hard-coded message burst when the matching chat opens. Audience questions cover WhatsApp Web request replay, NLP replies, and Android 13 changes.

The closing ties the hobby project to conference relevance: banking malware and spyware widely abuse accessibility services to read pins, hijack apps, and bypass sandboxing, often with little on-screen warning. She urges reviewing which apps hold accessibility permissions, notes the technique generalizes beyond WhatsApp, and briefly mentions USB keyboard emulation as another automation path.

talks.title: 0Day Up Your Sleeve Attacking macOS Environments by Wojciech Reguła | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: A macOS red-team chain covers Mythic C2, Gatekeeper bypass, sandbox escape, persistence, and theft from VPN, AD, Signal, and browsers.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that Macs are now commonplace in enterprises—especially among developers—yet often sit outside MDM, run stale operating system versions, and receive far less hardening than Windows fleets. It sketches three corporate integration models: Macs bound to Active Directory, Macs using Kerberos helpers such as Nomad without binding, and cloud-centric single sign-on without on-premises directory services. Assessments reportedly find disabled firewalls, absent application allowlisting, admin-by-default users, and finance or iOS teams on unmanaged hardware.

The demonstrated attack chain uses the Mythic framework against a Mac on OpenVPN with Nomad, AWS credentials, Firefox, and Signal. Initial access options include notarized payloads, social engineering around unsigned disk images, Gatekeeper bypass research, Word macros, a reboot-dependent Word sandbox escape, and an undisclosed zero day that breaks standard macOS sandboxing without reboot. After callback, persistence is established with launch agents. Collection walks through OpenVPN profile abuse and dynamic library injection for VPN passwords, Nomad Active Directory secrets from the keychain without elevation, plaintext Signal database keys in application support, default Firefox password stores, TCC bypass to harvest contacts and iMessage, and non-TCC cloud or SSH material under the home directory.

Recommendations close with MDM enrollment, patching, enforced System Integrity Protection, disabling Office macros, endpoint protection, and monitoring. Audience questions address quarantine behavior for Word documents, how the TCC proof of concept behaved, and whether virtual-desktop-only Mac usage still leaves gaps.

talks.title: CXO Panel | IoT Supply Chain Blues And The Way Forward | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Industry panelists debate IoT supply chain risk, vendor trust, and the baseline controls that matter.
talks.summary:
This CXO-style panel asked whether IoT supply chain risk is a real threat or hype. The panelists, from semiconductor, industrial, medical and energy backgrounds, agreed it is already happening. One cited a 217 percent rise in attacks on IoT devices over the last year, and noted that an earlier major breach began at an HVAC provider. Industrial devices that sense and actuate make compromise a physical matter.

Discussion of what is missing centred on vendor visibility. Panelists wanted a software bill of materials or component list from every downstream supplier, plus firmware development held to the same discipline as secure development lifecycles. One proposed trusted boot with signature checks based on NIST-approved algorithms, combined with device attestation so an app can confirm a device is genuine. Another recommended threat modelling per device class and third-party testing. Cost pressure ran through everything: unique key provisioning adds manufacturing expense, and crypto agility and post-quantum planning matter for devices expected to last decades.

Audience questions covered whether consumers should pay more for secure devices, with the answer that spending should match the device's role, and how to protect equipment meant to last 50 years, where panelists conceded that updating PKI in the field is slow. Late in the session, monitoring came up: IoT assets must be recorded with owner and location data, and IT and OT monitoring centres are converging. Closing takeaways were building IoT and embedded skills, agreeing standards with vendors, defining responsibility for incidents, and building trust from the ground up.

talks.title: c0ntextomy Lets Debug Together by Nikias Bassen | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: A technical breakdown shows how plain-text iOS wireless debug traffic lets network attackers hijack LLDB sessions for remote code execution.
talks.summary:
The presentation walks through Apple’s lockdown daemon and how host tools start iOS device services over USB and Wi‑Fi. After iOS 13, service startup is supposed to use SSL everywhere, yet wireless and even USB debugging can complete a handshake and then speak in cleartext because the on-device debug server never adopts the encrypted socket that lockdown hands to other services. The speaker traces that mismatch through the mobile device framework, Xcode’s plugin path, and the LLDB RPC bridge, framing it as an architectural carryover from wire-only development.

Research began from reports that libimobiledevice could not debug once Apple enforced SSL on USB. Packet captures confirmed plaintext GDB remote traffic on the LAN. The exploit chain assumes an attacker on the same network who can redirect traffic, while a developer runs wireless debugging. The talk describes spotting the debug TCP flow, waiting until Xcode receives process-profiling telemetry, pausing the target without alerting the victim, and attaching a second LLDB client—ultimately via a file-descriptor handoff—to seize the session and run unsigned code through debugger expressions, with a modular proof-of-concept for exfiltration.

Disclosure to Apple stretched across betas and advisory writing; initial Xcode fixes introduced a fallback that allowed downgrading to the legacy insecure debug service on iOS 13.6 and 13.7 under MITM conditions. Apple later shipped encrypted debug and instruments tunnel services on iOS 14 and watchOS 7, aligned with how the open-source tooling was patched. Practitioners should treat wireless debugging as sensitive on untrusted networks and understand that client-side SSL without end-to-end service adoption leaves a high-impact LAN attack surface.

talks.title: CXO Panel | Does Your SOC Suck? | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Panelists examine how to judge SOC maturity, from visibility gaps and ATT&CK coverage to where AI fits.
talks.summary:
The panel asks what a Security Operations Center is for and how to judge whether one is mature. Panelists describe the SOC as the first line of defense, meant to spot malicious activity early, and stress visibility that goes beyond network and endpoint data to include business locations, standalone firewalls that never reach a central console, and infrastructure changes that IT must share with security. One panelist warns that a SIM should not become a store for logs; use cases tied to business risk should drive what gets collected.

On maturity, the discussion centres on the MITRE ATT&CK framework. The panelists note that version 11 lists 14 tactics and 222 techniques, and that saying you have adopted it does not mean detections exist for every technique, since some depend on controls such as endpoint or network DLP. Basic gaps they mention include internet-facing firewall rules that allow any source, destination and service, and servers where OS-level logging is never enabled. Using WannaCry as an example, they argue that a SOC can write detection rules for the SMB1 ports while patching catches up.

Looking ahead, panelists agree that machine learning helps with analysis at scale. One cites a machine learning rule in Sentinel, called Fusion, that covers 120 scenarios that would otherwise need many static rules. All reject the idea of a SOC run without people, since automated responses can cause outages. The pandemic's remote-access surge also strained on-prem SIM licensing. The closing advice is to start from business objectives, define use cases and involve security in change management.

talks.title: Hacking 5G Is No Rocket Science by Altaf Shaik & Matteo Strada | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how insecure 5G service APIs on IoT SIM platforms leaked customer data and reached connected devices.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how 5G moves core network functions onto standardized APIs, exposing a network interface to vertical industries, third parties and cloud providers. The speakers explain how a customer can buy IoT SIM cards, get access to a connectivity management platform and use service APIs to query device location, send downlink SMS or IP messages, change sleep modes and billing counters, and even upload a new SIM master key.

To assess these platforms, the researchers built business relationships with nine or ten operators and bought SIM cards. They said registration could be done by submitting a company's public tax ID, which made it possible to pose as another company. Across the platforms they reported weak password rules that were only checked at account creation, long-lived or shared static tokens, and little or no rate limiting, with 400 requests sent without any back-off or IP ban. Verbose errors let them probe IMSI, ICCID and IMEI values, script injection worked on six of ten platforms, and a restricted test profile could still reach sensitive gateway addresses. A webhook response also leaked SIM and core network details, IP messages reached devices belonging to other industries, and a known malware sample sent by SMS was delivered without filtering.

The speakers conclude that 5G is more secure than earlier generations, but exposed APIs make the network a more attractive target. They recommend secure design, standard OAuth and TLS practice, strong password and token policies, and generic error messages. They also suggested that a Telecom API top 10 could emerge in the coming years.

talks.title: CXO Panel | Securing India The CERTIn Way | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss CERT-In's incident reporting and KYC directions and what they mean for organisations and CISOs.
talks.summary:
The panel, held at Nullcon Goa 2022, looked at CERT-In's recent directions for India's security community and the intent behind them. Dr. Behl opened with the threat picture: a sharp rise in reported threats over 2021, attackers abusing tools already present in victim networks such as remote administration software and reverse proxies, and intrusions that went unnoticed because logs and monitoring were missing. He argued that timely reporting lets responders contain an attack, and that a round-the-clock point of contact is essential.

Anupriya Daga said banks already work to a four-to-six-hour reporting window and find shared indicators useful, though other sectors are still maturing. Ajit Menon agreed that actionable intelligence matters more than raw indicators, but questioned several requirements: time synchronisation for every system including operational technology, identity checks for VPN and hosting customers, and how service providers should report when a client is the affected party. Concerns about log retention becoming surveillance also came up.

Dr. Behl replied that accurate timestamps are essential for cross-border investigations, that continuity plans should assume loss of connectivity, and that KYC can be done in several ways rather than through Aadhaar alone. He said enforcement would follow real incidents, that a list of reportable incidents already exists, and that further FAQs were in process. The session closed with CERT-In's responsible disclosure programme and its role as a CVE numbering authority.

talks.title: CXO Panel | PAM Maturity From Zero Trust To Least Privilege | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Panelists discuss how privileged access management supports zero trust and moves organisations toward least privilege.
talks.summary:
This panel, led by a moderator, explores privileged access management (PAM) and its path from zero trust to least privilege. Panelists describe privileged credentials as the keys to core systems, used mostly by administrators, developers and operations staff. Rolling out PAM is as much a cultural change as a technical one, requiring management buy-in, trained staff, documented procedures and coverage across on-premises, cloud, hybrid and OT estates. A breach report cited during the session links 61 percent of compromised credentials to privileged accounts.

On zero trust, PAM verifies the user, the device and the session before granting access, while logging, recording and flagging anomalies against an organisational baseline. Panelists warn that PAM alone prevents nothing without its prerequisites and complementary controls. Compliance is treated as a necessary mandate, but risk-based thinking, with defined normal patterns such as approved change windows, makes deviations easier to spot. Expected next-generation features include container and cloud support, centralised key management, one-time tokens, offboarding through directory integration and dependency mapping.

For least privilege, the panel argues against standing access. Users sign in with minimal rights, elevate for routine tasks, and request approval for sensitive command groups, while the most dangerous commands are blocked outright. Workflow approvals and session accountability are presented as ways to reduce insider misuse and support audits. The closing advice is that no single architecture fits every organisation: start with critical assets, segment them, then work down the risk tiers and review the plan regularly.

talks.title: Elevating The TrustZone To Achieve A Powerful Android Kernel Exploit | Tamir Zahavi Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how a Qualcomm TrustZone communication bug lets an Android app gain arbitrary kernel memory read and write.
talks.summary:
Android phones run a second, higher-privileged operating system called TrustZone, which holds keys for things like DRM and is almost always closed source. This talk examines Qualcomm's implementation, which shares memory with the Android kernel through a kernel module and ION buffers. Shared regions are described by physical addresses and a whitelist that tells the secure side what memory it may touch.

The bug lies in how the kernel builds those whitelist entries. Because a user process supplies buffer references with offsets, overlapping offsets can overwrite an address so the secure side whitelists arbitrary physical memory, including kernel memory. Non-contiguous buffers then let the attacker control both the address and the size of the whitelisted region. Getting a usable command out of a DRM trustlet required heavy reversing; two of its functions shared one symmetric key for encryption and decryption, so they could act as a memory copy. That gave arbitrary kernel read and write, and kernel symbols were located by scanning memory, letting the exploit disable SELinux across several devices and builds without per-build changes.

The exploit needs the Qualcomm kernel module, which is normally out of reach for apps, though a previously published service bug could bridge that gap. Physical addresses are not randomized, and the attack is data-only, so it sidesteps code-execution mitigations and may survive memory tagging. The takeaways: closed-source secure components and physical-memory primitives deserve more research, and the vendor fix added a check against overlapping data. A write-up and source code were promised.

talks.title: Software Defined Snort With Barnyard & Pulled Pork For NIDPS by Arun Baskaran | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Maps SDN learning switches to Snort, Barnyard, and Pulled Pork for automated NIDPS defense against volumetric and application floods.
talks.summary:
The talk outlines a long-running project that embeds open-source network intrusion detection and prevention into a software-defined networking stack so defensive policy can change with traffic instead of relying on hands-on rule churn. The speaker opens with SDN and OpenFlow as a way to program switches, Mininet for lab emulation, and controllers such as Floodlight, Ryu, and POX when hardware is scarce.

Snort sits at the center, with Barnyard added because Snort’s single-threaded design struggles at high packet rates, and Pulled Pork described as a small automation layer that refreshes rules when public repositories publish new issues. The middle of the session walks a three-plane management-switch model—application analytics, a control plane built from five-tuple rules and learning-switch behavior versus hub flooding, and a data plane where Intel DPDK is proposed to keep pace with very large floods. Snort’s decoder, preprocessors, detection engine, and logging are shown running in parallel with switch-level blocks by flow, packet size, or sustained source rate.

Later segments classify volumetric, protocol, and application-layer denial-of-service patterns and argue that programmable control can catch insiders bypassing vendor appliances. Unified security policies, logging, and reduced manual feed maintenance are framed as operational wins. Questions address preprocessor tailoring, staffing or APIs for rule ingestion, Suricata as a possible substitute, and why CAPTCHA alone may not save an application under heavy automated request load.

talks.title: CXO Panel | Unlocking Security Collaboration With Cyber Threat Intelligence | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Security leaders on a panel weigh how threat intelligence fits strategy, from IOC blocklists to behavioral detection and trust.
talks.summary:
The panel opens by placing cyber threat intelligence alongside prevention, detection and response, as the predictive pillar that tells defenders what is coming. The panelists compare it with state intelligence work and stress that intelligence must be timely, relevant and actionable, and that it expires. Each speaker sees it feeding firewalls, proxies, detection platforms and forensic work, with the real difficulty being how to judge which feeds to trust.

The middle of the session looks at indicators of compromise. One telecom-side speaker described feeds that asked for whole countries or address pools to be blocked, which could cut off roaming users and customers, and a second recalled an address blocked for months that later hosted a vendor's operating system updates. Attackers can cheaply change domains and file hashes, so the group argued for tracking tactics and behaviour instead. They also described scoring intelligence dynamically and correlating outside feeds with an organisation's own telemetry. On collaboration, they noted that regulators and national response teams have built trusted sharing channels, while companies still hesitate to disclose breaches. Audience questions covered cloud visibility gaps, false positives and interoperable standards.

The closing message is that threat intelligence only works alongside people, process, technology and governance. Practitioners should prioritise intelligence by relevance to their own environment, validate it against internal data, and choose tools that support common exchange standards.

talks.title: Do PDF Tools Conform To The Specification by Prashant Anantharaman
talks.teaser: Shows that popular PDF extractors disagree on the same file and presents Sparta tooling to validate and repair spec violations.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by arguing that parser validation matters for security: crafted documents often trigger bugs, and three common text-extraction tools produce visibly different output on one SEC filing despite all targeting PDF 1.7. That mismatch illustrates parser differentials, linked to past certificate parsing issues and iOS entitlement XML handling, and motivates language-theoretic security principles such as full recognition before processing, rejecting malformed input, and separating parsers from application logic.

The speaker walks through PDF structure—header, objects, trailer, cross-reference table, and catalog dictionary—and contrasts wild files with the machine-readable DOM maintained by the PDF Association. The Parsley project and Sparta implement Rust code generated from that DOM, with a breadth-first type checker that flagged inconsistencies in the spec itself before validation could succeed. Live demos flag missing page-tree and page parent keys, then apply reducer rules so the document still opens and metadata such as author fields becomes readable.

A large crawl-scale evaluation highlights recurring errors: bad language keys that break extraction, page-tree problems that block rendering, layout keys, and dangling references, with LaTeX-generated PDFs overrepresented among font-related faults. Practitioners should treat spec conformance as operational hygiene: normalize PDFs to reduce differentials, use strict checking where feasible, and expect the ecosystem to keep weakening the standard when major implementations diverge.

talks.title: CXO Panel | Cloud Services For Financial Inclusion Possibilities And Challenges | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Government, banking and cloud speakers weigh how cloud can widen financial inclusion in India and the security trade-offs.
talks.summary:
The panel opened with the framing of financial inclusion in India and a central bank index built on 97 parameters. A government cybersecurity official credited broadband rollout and a rise in bank accounts, to about 109 crore, and said cloud-native payment firms cut costs and reduced reliance on foreign card networks. A bank technology leader said cloud gives small and large lenders similar tools, narrowing the gap between them.

The discussion then turned to regulation and control. The regulator's draft guidance on IT outsourcing includes a cloud annex covering vendor selection, data sovereignty and exit planning. The official said critical-sector entities should use empanelled providers, keep encryption keys under their own control, and close gaps between provider and customer monitoring. A bank speaker warned teams to map who handles each part of the data flow instead of relying on labels such as IaaS or SaaS, and to build a standard landing zone first. A cloud-born company said it went through about 70 iterations before launch and automated its compliance controls.

In audience questions, a speaker raised phishing and OTP fraud hitting new digital users with little technical knowledge. The official said feedback from law enforcement to regulators has led to controls such as alerts on large transactions. The panel closed on user education, clear shared responsibility with providers, and disciplined cloud adoption.

talks.title: Raining CVEs On WordPress Plugins With Semgrep by Shreya Pohekar & Sheeraz Ali | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Semgrep rules scan WordPress plugins for injection flaws, reduce false positives, and deliver automated fuzzing and CVE reporting.
talks.summary:
The speakers frame their work under Code Vigilant: improve open-source security by finding and fixing flaws, or responsibly warning when projects are abandoned but still in use. They targeted WordPress because its ecosystem includes more than 80,000 plugins and PHP-centric code suits large-scale static review.

They paired Semgrep with iterative rule writing—starting from simple XSS and SQLi patterns, adding ellipsis between sources and sinks, and building exclusion lists for common WordPress sanitizers. Manual confirmation on initial SQLi hits motivated automation: modules that test injections across WordPress role levels, diff crawls between clean and plugin installs to surface reachable URLs, and templated reporting for WPScan and Code Vigilant. Thousands of possible XSS findings led to XSSBomb, which parses Semgrep output, installs plugins on a resettable base VM, and fuzzes only flagged parameters with gxss—far faster than per-plugin Vagrant or Docker churn.

They illustrate why sanitize_text_field and similar helpers often fail across HTML, URL, or SQL contexts, contrast weak single filters with nested encoding, and note WP Magic Quotes as a stubborn barrier. The effort produced on the order of 47–48 confirmed issues with CVE assignments. They outline next steps: themes, other PHP CMS platforms, LFI/SSRF/RCE rule sets, SVN chunking so Semgrep can handle massive trees, and evolving XSSBomb into a broader vulnerability validator.

talks.title: Mind The Gap - The Linux Ecosystem Kernel Patch Gap by Jakob Lell & Regina Bíró | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Explores why Linux kernel CVE fixes often miss end-user devices and introduces an automated tool to find missing patches.
talks.summary:
Consumer and industrial gear often outlives the security updates vendors ship. The presenters open with recent privilege-escalation and remote takeover kernel issues, using Dirty Pipe as an example: the flaw may have existed for years while fixes landed only in select upstream versions, leaving many forked or backlevel trees exposed unless someone manually backports.

They walk through how patching chains together Linux upstream, Android common kernel sources, chipset vendors such as Qualcomm, and per-device drivers. Cited research and their own statistics highlight delays and volume—on the order of a hundred disclosed issues in half a year, with a large share tied to chipset-specific disclosure. Fragmentation forces manual backports; choosing non-LTS kernels or losing chipset support mid-lifecycle can make full patching impractical. European rules now push clearer support windows, yet enforcement has lagged.

The core contribution is an automated analyzer that maps CVEs to patch commits from bulletins and public git sources, then tests trees by applying and reverting patches, with optional build instrumentation to skip irrelevant components and architecture filtering to cut noise. Optimizations yield roughly sub-minute runs across hundreds of CVEs on large machines. Released via Docker, it targets security auditors and device vendors as a pre-release sanity check. Automation cannot fix fragmentation or short support policies, but it can surface gaps vendors might otherwise miss.

talks.title: Goa 2022 | Scale Hacking To Secure Your Cloud And Beyond by Anand Prakash
talks.teaser: Walks through bug bounty case studies where small flaws were chained into account takeovers and cloud compromises.
talks.summary:
The talk presents bug bounty case studies in which several small flaws were chained into high-impact results. At Tinder, sign-in relied on Facebook's Account Kit phone login. The speaker found a hidden endpoint, referenced in the dashboard's JavaScript, for changing a phone number that never checked the new number against the confirmation code. That let an attacker obtain a session cookie for any Account Kit user, and Tinder's API accepted it to take over accounts.

At Uber, a driver sign-up flow returned an internal user ID for any phone number or email entered. A separate consent-screen RPC call then exposed that user's mobile access token, which worked across the app's APIs. The speaker also described a Facebook issue, not yet publicly disclosed, where an access token from the main app let authorized third-party apps reach messages and account data despite only basic permissions. The cloud section covered an open Docker registry whose images contained hardcoded AWS keys, and CloudFormation templates that exposed Jira, Slack and GitHub tokens. A developer's AWS key pushed to a public repository gave full control over EC2, RDS and S3 for a crypto platform within a minute; the key was deactivated two days after the disclosure.

The takeaways are to chain low-severity findings, test main applications rather than stopping at reconnaissance, and learn how backends and infrastructure work instead of relying on automated tools. Persistence matters, and researchers should stay within permission and ethical limits.

talks.title: Hack the Source: Securing OSS - One Bug At A Time by Sandeep Singh | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how to pick an open source target, review its code and claim rewards through the Internet Bug Bounty.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that open source projects need more researchers reading their code, and shows how bug bounty programs can reward that work. Modern software is built on open source components, including dependencies of dependencies, and community contributors maintain much of it. Targets can be found by filtering HackerOne's opportunities by source code, which surfaces company-run programs as well as vulnerability disclosure programs for projects such as Kubernetes, curl and Node.js.

The suggested approach is to focus on one project for a long stretch rather than hunting across the whole open source pool. Before reading code, set up an editor with project-wide and regex search, learn the language, and build a threat model around key functionality. Static analysis tools such as CodeQL, LGTM, Brakeman, SpotBugs and cppcheck can generate leads, but their output still needs reading and test code and trusted inputs can be excluded. Manual review should target trust boundaries, authentication, serialization, complex or old code, and areas written by developers whose changes often introduced bugs.

The talk then introduces the Internet Bug Bounty, which pools funds from sponsors including Figma, Facebook, TikTok, Elastic and Shopify to pay for bugs in enrolled projects. Rewards are split 80/20 between the finder and the project, and a published advisory or CVE is needed before claiming. If a maintainer does not respond, the speaker suggests waiting roughly 30 to 90 days before contacting the program. The takeaway is to build fundamentals first, since smaller projects often lack resources to fix what is reported.

talks.title: ElectroVolt Pwning Desktop Apps Built On Electron by Mohan Sri Rama | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Shows how Electron desktop apps like VS Code and Teams can be taken over via XSS, misconfigured web preferences and V8 exploits.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Electron, the framework that lets developers build cross-platform desktop apps with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and explains how its main process and renderer process differ. It then covers the web preferences that govern the renderer, including sandboxing, node integration, preload scripts and context isolation, and shows how weaker settings let a script injection reach the operating system.

Case studies follow. In VS Code, a malicious markdown file in an untrusted folder led to a chain of cross-origin navigation and postMessage misconfigurations that reached a window with node integration enabled. In Discord, a cross-site scripting flaw in an embedded frame was combined with an error in how Electron initialised new windows, and a V8 bug was then used to run code in a window without sandboxing. In Microsoft Teams, a zero-day in an editor component was used to pollute prototypes and leak internal IPC, which could read a local file and expose a user's authentication token. Other cases involve node integration in subframes and disabled context isolation, where V8 exploits flipped configuration bits in the renderer.

The takeaways are practical. Keep sandboxing on, disable node integration and enable context isolation, and avoid exposing privileged IPC channels or the legacy remote module. Restrict XSS and open-redirect routing, including on subdomains, and keep Electron updated, since its V8 and Chromium components tend to lag behind the Chrome browser.

talks.title: A Kernel Hacker Meets Fuchsia OS | Alexander Popov | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Details Zircon microkernel attacks on Fuchsia: timer UAF, vtable hijacks, kernel-log flaws, and syscall-table rootkit escalation.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces Google's Fuchsia OS and its Zircon microkernel, contrasting capability-based security and a reduced in-kernel surface with a still large syscall interface and strong component sandboxing. The speaker describes building and running Fuchsia in QEMU, debugging similarly to Linux, and validating Kernel Address Sanitizer with a deliberate timer use-after-free bug.

Fuzzing with syzkaller proved impractical after broken upstream integration, so work focused on weaponizing that synthetic bug. A FIFO-based heap spray replaces the freed timer dispatcher; blind experimentation on C++ object layout enables vtable abuse for kernel control flow. Separate findings include improper kernel-log access when passing a zero resource ID and non-functional KASLR on tested builds. With SMEP and SMAP turned off in the emulator for the demo, a fake vtable redirects execution into attacker code.

Privilege escalation without a root user leads to overwriting the syscall table—classic CR0 write-protect clearing—and hooking process creation while neutering assert paths. The demo prints rootkit messages when uname runs. Practitioners should expect microkernel compromises to chain through IPC and capabilities rather than local root, and that responsible disclosure yielded assigned CVEs plus renewed fuzzing support and bug bounty scope.

talks.title: Hack The Bridge by Anto Joseph | Nullcon Goa 2022
talks.teaser: Explains blockchain bridge designs and walks through smart contract exploits used against real bridges, now patched.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with blockchain basics for a newer audience: a chain is a shared list of transactions, and Ethereum adds distributed execution of smart contracts. Because native assets such as Ether cannot move directly to another chain, bridges represent them as tokens on the destination. The speaker contrasts a centralized custodial wrapped-token model with message-passing bridges that rely on off-chain relayers, validators and watchers. The speaker then compares cross-chain and multi-chain designs and their trade-offs, including chain reorganizations that can double-credit funds.

Next the speaker reviews where bridge losses come from. Many of the largest incidents involved stolen private keys rather than contract code, and bugs in MPC protocols and proof systems are also a concern. Two demonstrations follow. In the first, a multi-chain bridge let the caller supply the token address. An attacker-written contract returned a wrapped token, and a permit call to a token without that function did not revert, so approved user funds could be drained. In the second, a Nomad-style replica was initialized with a zero committed root. An upgrade turned root checking into a map lookup, so the zero default was accepted and invalid withdrawals went through.

The closing advice for developers is to follow verification standards, use audited libraries and write invariant tests. White-hat researchers were pointed to a set of tools. The Q&A closes with an explanation of reentrancy.

talks.title: Keynote | Do we get stuff done? We don’t get stuff done? Or do we? Or will we? | Mario Heiderich
talks.teaser: A keynote contrasts breakthrough public-health ideas with stubborn web flaws and argues for secure-by-default browser and framework design.
talks.summary:
Mario Heiderich frames a two-part story about whether the web security community actually finishes what it starts. The first half argues that familiar classes such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting persist for decades despite simple fixes, unlike CSRF after SameSite cookies became a default browser behavior. Historical parallels—Jenner, Semmelweis, Carson, and Mike West—illustrate how single bold interventions can eliminate whole categories of harm, while reactive patching and optional controls have failed to do the same for injection flaws.

The second half highlights momentum toward “impossible by design” defenses: Trusted Types to block risky DOM string sinks, and Element.setHTML (developed with Google collaborators and tied to DOMPurify’s lineage) to sanitize HTML assignments in the browser. He describes industry pushback when these ship, but also growing adoption as vendors enforce safer defaults.

Practitioners are urged to deprioritize endless compatibility with unsafe legacy patterns, invest in platform-enforced hygiene rather than voluntary hardening alone, and push frameworks and languages so developers cannot easily write raw queries or unsanitized markup. The closing message is optimism that XSS and SQL injection could follow CSRF toward practical extinction if the field shifts from patch stacks to design that makes entire bug classes unreachable.

talks.title: Reversing and De-Obfuscating Malware with Software Emulation | Nullcon Webinar 2022
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Reversing and De-Obfuscating Malware with Software Emulation | Nullcon Webinar 2022.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this Nullcon Webinar 2022 presentation, security researcher Chiziar Fidzi explores how software emulation can be used to reverse engineer and de-obfuscate malware. Hosted by Sakshi from the Nullcon team, the webinar contrasts software emulation against traditional full-OS sandboxing (such as Cuckoo, Anubis, or Joe Sandbox). While a sandbox runs malware within an actual operating system, emulation constructs a simulated OS environment around the binary using engines like Unicorn and Speakeasy. This approach gives analysts fine-grained control to inspect API calls, bypass network failures, instrument instructions, and force execution down specific paths.

### Key Topics
- **Emulation vs. Sandboxing**: Understanding the distinction between detonating malware in a live VM and emulating hardware/OS structures (such as TEB/PEB via Python engines) to achieve deep code instrumentation.
- **Overcoming Infrastructure Downtime**: Faking network and API responses when external Command and Control (C2) servers or domains are already dead.
- **De-obfuscating Control Flow Flattening**: Resolving complex dispatcher loops, switch/state machines, and opaque execution flows by inspecting and instrumenting CPU registers.
- **Analyzing In-Memory Evasion**: Tracking API hooks and memory dumps to identify unhooking techniques aimed at evading EDR/antivirus tools.

### Technical Details
The speaker uses Ghidra for static analysis alongside his Python-based tool **Resploit** (RispR0it), which builds upon Unicorn and Speakeasy.

1. **Case 1: Excel Macro Shellcode Extraction & Emulation**
   - A malicious Excel macro extracts an array of bytes, creates a buffer via `VirtualAlloc`, and executes shellcode using `CreateThread`.
   - Running Resploit’s `emulate payload` command reveals process injection: a suspended `rundll32.exe` process is spawned via `CreateProcess`, memory is written, and execution continues via `CreateRemoteThread`.
   - Unlike full sandbox runs (e.g., Any.run), which stalled at unresolved DNS queries for `shinyobjects.birds`, the emulator simulates network functions, dumping a second-stage payload (`metal.exe` saved locally as `chrome.exe`). Resploit dumps thread memory using the `-t` flag and skips long sleep cycles automatically.

2. **Case 2: De-obfuscating a Flattened Ramnit / Bumblebee DLL**
   - The target is an x86 DLL lacking standard exports, requiring execution via `DllMain` (`DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH`).
   - The malware utilizes `MapViewOfFile` to map `ntdll.dll` into memory. In an emulator, missing OS files must be provided in the tool's filesystem directory to avoid path errors.
   - Ghidra reveals heavy control flow flattening (a complex state machine driven by nested `while` loops and the `EAX` register).
   - By inserting Python instrumentation into the emulation script at address `32B6`, the speaker logs the values of `EAX` at the start of loop iterations, effectively unrolling the flattened control flow.
   - Tracking the unrolled state reveals the loop searches for the export `NtProtectVirtualMemory` within the mapped `ntdll.dll`.
   - Using Resploit's `-m` flag (dumping memory allocations on read, execute, or free), the speaker captures the allocated buffer before the function breaks. Cross-referencing the dumped memory in PE-bear confirms the malware is copying a clean version of `NtProtectVirtualMemory` directly into memory to bypass EDR/AV userland hooks.

### Takeaways
- Emulation offers unparalleled control over code flow, letting analysts trace internal registers, modify branch execution, and dump unpacked memory buffers on demand.
- While emulation encounters performance bottlenecks with repetitive loops (making it substantially slower than bare-metal execution), it provides critical advantages when dealing with offline C2 infrastructure, complex API unhooking, and control flow flattening.

talks.title: Introduction to the OWASP ModSecurity Core Rule Set | Christian Folini | Nullcon Webinar
talks.teaser: Explains how the OWASP ModSecurity Core Rule Set works as a first line of web application defense.
talks.summary:
Christian Folini introduces the OWASP ModSecurity Core Rule Set, a broad collection of deny rules that runs on the ModSecurity engine inside a web server such as Apache or Nginx. He frames a web application firewall as a seat belt: a baseline layer that buys time and makes attacks harder, not a complete fix that replaces secure coding or patching.

In one test, a scanner reported over a thousand requests hitting weaknesses in a deliberately vulnerable app, and a five-minute CRS install mitigated more than 80 percent of them. A blog comparison of cloud WAF services found CRS-based offerings blocked more payloads, and a Black Hat Asia study, cited in a news report, gave CRS a 97 percent block rate against AWS's 37 percent. Folini then explains paranoia levels one to four, which trade stronger detection for more false positives, and anomaly scoring, which separates detection from blocking so teams can lower the threshold step by step. A live sandbox demo showed a local file inclusion request being reported with triggered rule IDs and a total score of 10.

The talk then turns to false positives, which are handled with rule exclusions scoped to a URI, parameter or rule. Major releases come about once a year so enterprises can retest, plugins add extras such as Lua-based functions, and Coraza may become a drop-in engine as ModSecurity's developers step back. Folini suggests mod_qos or a CDN for anti-automation, and closes by stressing that CRS is one layer in a holistic security posture.

talks.title: Ransomware Considered Hazardous To Your Health | Nullcon Webinars 2022
talks.teaser: Reframes ransomware as an extortion business, using leak-site data and Conti chats to test common assumptions about attackers.
talks.summary:
The talk takes a government advisory on the rising ransomware threat and uses it as a framework for checking against the speaker's own data. Charles van der Walt of Orange Cyber Defense draws on leak-site records of more than 4,000 victims tracked over about two years, the Conti chat leak of roughly 200,000 messages, and about 34,000 confirmed incidents from a managed detection service.

The data suggests the problem is global but shifting: victims cluster in large English-speaking economies, yet are moving toward bigger non-English markets such as China, Japan and India, which the speaker links to language and cultural barriers for the actors. Manufacturing is the most affected sector, and extortion methods are diversifying, though only a small share of cases use them. The speaker argues the crime is cyber extortion rather than a malware problem, that attackers harvest opportunistic victims rather than hunt big-game targets, and that incident volumes follow victim working patterns as much as attacker ones.

The conclusion is that basic hygiene such as patching, unique passwords and privileged-access control is sound but will not stop the crime alone. The speaker recommends reducing the flow of funds to criminals, making victims less attractive by cutting attack surface, and investing in response and recovery with tested plans.

talks.title: Cloud Security Posture Management & Threat Protection | Suman & Sakaldeep | Nullcon Webinars 2022
talks.teaser: Explains cloud posture management and workload threat protection, then demos Microsoft Defender for Cloud on Azure.
talks.summary:
This workshop by Suman Tiwari and Sakaldeep, part of the Nullcon webinar series, covers cloud security posture management (CSPM) and cloud workload protection. CSPM tools continuously compare a cloud environment against best-practice rules to flag misconfigurations and compliance gaps, rather than relying on periodic scans. Secure scores, recommendations and built-in or custom policies show teams where they stand and what to fix, and some vendors can apply fixes automatically.

The threat protection side, also called cloud workload protection, watches live traffic and logs on resources such as virtual machines, databases and containers, flagging suspicious activity with threat intelligence, behaviour analysis and anomaly detection. Alerts can be sent to a SIEM or wired into automated workflows, such as a logic app that blocks an attacking IP address. The presenters also tied these checks to standards like PCI DSS, CIS benchmarks and NIST.

The live demo used Microsoft Defender for Cloud on Azure across 84 resources, where the secure score was 38. Findings included MFA not enabled on accounts, RDP open to any source, subnets without a network security group, unencrypted VM disks and missing endpoint protection. Alerts for brute-force RDP attempts from attacker IPs, file integrity changes and adaptive application control were then reviewed, and a workflow was shown blocking an attacking address automatically. The session ended with Q&A on the CIS benchmark and on choosing tools for multi-cloud setups.

talks.title: What is Cyber Threat Intelligence | Rishika Desai | Winja Unplugged
talks.teaser: Introduces cyber threat intelligence through a researcher's daily work, tracking threat actors, and staying anonymous online.
talks.summary:
This session, given as part of an online unplugged series, introduces cyber threat intelligence to people with little or no background in the field. The speaker, a cyber threat researcher, describes CTI as gathering and analysing information about existing and emerging threats so that organisations can make informed decisions. She separates three kinds of intelligence: strategic (non-technical trends, geopolitics and statistics), tactical (the techniques and procedures attackers use to get in and operate) and operational (machine-readable indicators such as malware samples, domains and IP addresses).

The talk then follows a researcher's daily routine. It covers monitoring underground forums, marketplaces selling ransomware builders and stolen data, and new leak sites or domains. Two examples show how posts can be pieced together into a story: a ransomware affiliate recruitment advert, and a forum listing of internal logs from a bank after a victim reportedly refused to pay. The speaker stresses linking posts over time into a timeline to anticipate what a group may do next, and introduces the MITRE ATT&CK knowledge base as a way to map adversary behaviour to detection and defence. Useful skills named include research, analytical thinking, interest in malware and a basic understanding of vulnerabilities.

A large part of the talk covers protecting the researcher's own anonymity. Suggested measures include working in virtual machines, routing traffic through Tor-based systems and VPNs, and never reusing usernames or credentials across sources. The speaker also warns against clicking links sent by threat actors, citing reported cases in which researchers were threatened or had personal data leaked. The closing advice is that a career in CTI rests more on curiosity, persistence and staying current with threat news and sources than on certification.

talks.title: CVE-2018-9206 Workshop | Sanjay Das | Winja Unplugged
talks.teaser: Shows how the jQuery File Upload flaw CVE-2018-9206 works in a Docker lab, and how its patches were bypassed.
talks.summary:
The session covers CVE-2018-9206, an unauthenticated arbitrary file upload flaw in the jQuery File Upload project, which the speaker places in versions 9.2.0 and earlier. The root cause sat in Apache configuration. The AllowOverride directive was set to All before Apache 2.3.9 and defaulted to None afterwards, so the .htaccess rules meant to stop uploaded files from running were ignored.

The speaker rebuilt a vulnerable PHP 7.4 and Apache setup with Docker, uploaded a phpinfo file and showed it executing. The speaker then walked through the vendor's patches. The first added a server-side list of allowed extensions, which a multiple-extension file name got around when Apache mapped the PHP handler to several extensions. The next patch kept only the last extension, and the later check based on file magic bytes was bypassed through an ImageMagick flaw that let a script hide inside an image-like file. The demo ended by reading a password file through an uploaded script.

The takeaway is that each fix in the chain checked one property, such as the file name or the first bytes, while the server configuration still decided what ran. Defenders should confirm that upload directories cannot execute uploaded content, and that patches are tested against the bypasses that followed.

talks.title: Introduction to Threat Modeling | Siddhant Chouhan | Winja Unplugged
talks.teaser: Introduces STRIDE threat categories and shows how to model threats on a data flow diagram using OWASP Threat Dragon.
talks.summary:
The session introduces threat modeling as a security engineering activity used to spot threats and design or implementation weaknesses before software is built. It opens with a scenario: a retailer's smart air conditioning unit, owned by a third party, is compromised, and because the network was not segmented, the attacker can reach systems that hold customer card data. The speaker then walks through the STRIDE categories one by one, each with a simple example: spoofing a location to claim regional rewards, tampering with a message in transit, repudiating an email the sender never wrote, disclosing card details or personal data, exhausting resources to deny service, and escalating privileges by tampering with cookies under weak role-based access control.

The hands-on part uses OWASP Threat Dragon, a free open-source tool, to model an employee leave management web application. The presenter builds a data flow diagram with a client, the web application, a database, a configuration file holding credentials, and an internet trust boundary. Threats are attached to diagram elements with a status, priority, description and mitigation. Examples include unauthorized database access, mitigated by allow-listing addresses at a firewall, and an unencrypted configuration file, mitigated by encrypting it and rotating the database credentials. A sample report with a background worker and message queue shows how threats are grouped by category.

The takeaway is that the resulting report can be exported as a PDF and handed to engineers, who can use it while designing, coding and testing. Threat modeling in the design phase helps teams fix issues earlier in the development lifecycle, which saves time and cost.

talks.title: How to Master your CFP Submission by Review Board Members | Nullcon
talks.teaser: Review board members explain what weakens a CFP and how applicants can show clear technical depth instead of generic topics.
talks.summary:
Conference review board members answer questions about what makes call-for-papers submissions fail or feel unrewarding to score. They stress that reviewers need to see exactly what will be delivered: abstracts that stay vague, or that repeat the same material as the extended outline without adding clarity, leave the committee guessing whether the slot will hold a demo, a new attack, or a real problem-solving narrative.

Weak patterns include pitching broad tutorials on well-known attacks for a conference stage, reporting routine bounty findings without explaining non-obvious steps such as encoding chains, or offering theory without demonstrations. One reviewer compares unwanted entries to college paper competitions built from internet summaries. Large payout figures or familiar XSS at a major site do not substitute for the extra technical work that separates the talk from public write-ups or one-page blog posts.

Strong submissions sell a specific idea the way a strong job application does, with reasoning and technical meat visible upfront. Tool announcements belong in demo tracks unless the speaker teaches the methods behind the speedup or design. Applicants should foreground techniques reviewers cannot skim elsewhere, not command-line walkthroughs of yet another product.

talks.title: Bhadra framework: Threat modeling for mobile communication systems by Sid Rao | Nullcon Webinar 2021
talks.teaser: Presents Bhadra, a telco-specific threat modeling taxonomy inspired by MITRE ATT&CK, plus a web tool for annotating attacks.
talks.summary:
Sid Rao, a security researcher at Nokia Bell Labs, presents Bhadra, a threat modeling framework for mobile communication (telco) networks. He explains that telco systems combine radio access, core, service and operations networks built on very different technologies, which makes security events hard to describe in a shared way. Existing options fell short: STRIDE and PASTA proved of limited use, and MITRE ATT&CK centers on enterprise and platform threats.

Bhadra is presented as a common language and reference taxonomy of adversary tactics and techniques for telco, not an automated playbook or AI tool. The team catalogued public attacks, grouped them into tactics and techniques, and currently covers systems up to 4G. The first version listed 47 techniques, and the second expanded to 52. Attacks are organized into mounting, execution and impact, and standards misuse such as SS7 and GTP-based attacks gets its own category. A companion knowledge base stores descriptions, IDs, examples and mitigations, while an API and a web annotator let users model attacks and view them as attack graphs.

Sid outlines next steps: 5G coverage, a cautious scoring baseline that is indicative rather than a replacement for CVSS, recommendations, and attack emulation to test operator defenses. He invites feedback, data samples, tooling and research collaboration, since the work is early and meant to be community driven. For practitioners, the main takeaway is a shared vocabulary that supports detection, incident response, red teaming and defense mapping in telco environments.

talks.title: Red, Purple, and Blue team activity using Azure | Nullcon Workshop 2021 Suman & Sakaldeep
talks.teaser: Walks through attacking a containerized vulnerable web app, then detecting and blocking those attacks with Azure WAF and Sentinel.
talks.summary:
This workshop, given by Suman Tiwari and Sankaldeep Yadav, covers red, blue and purple team activity inside Microsoft Azure. The lab hosts DVWA, a deliberately vulnerable web application, in Azure Container Instances behind a web application firewall. The presenters first run attacks such as SQL injection and a file upload check bypass while the firewall only logs and does not block, then show those same requests recorded in Log Analytics through KQL queries.

They then switch the firewall to prevention mode, repeat the attacks, and show them being stopped. Azure Sentinel is used to pull in the firewall data, run analytics rules that raise incidents, assign those incidents to an analyst, and build workbook dashboards and hunting queries. The walkthrough also covers the managed rule set, custom rules, the 2 MB upload limit, and the steps for deploying the container and the application gateway.

Near the end the presenters list limits they found. At the time the firewall could not mitigate CSRF, and malicious file uploads were not covered by default rules, so a custom rule was needed. They also cover Azure Security Center, which scans resources against policies and gives recommendations and compliance views such as the CIS benchmark. The main takeaways are to tune rules in detection mode before enforcing them, centralise logs in a SIEM-style service, and handle CSRF in application code.

talks.title: The "crash" course, a non-programmer's guide to fuzzing | Rushikesh D. Nandedkar | Nullcon Webinar
talks.teaser: Shows non-programmers a hands-on fuzzing walkthrough against tcpdump, from instrumented builds to reading sanitizer crash reports.
talks.summary:
The session introduces fuzzing as an automated testing method that feeds an application unexpected or malformed inputs and watches for abnormal behaviour such as crashes, hangs or memory leaks. The speaker pitches the workshop at people with no programming background and explains why crashes matter most when hunting memory corruption bugs. The basic fuzzing loop, test case generation and the role of instrumentation are covered before the hands-on part begins.

Using tcpdump 4.8, an older release with known vulnerabilities, as the target, the speaker shows how to install dependencies on Ubuntu and build the program with AFL++ compiler wrappers. Sample capture files are trimmed with afl-cmin and checked with afl-analyze, and a run on overflow-triggering samples finds a crash. Rebuilding with AddressSanitizer turns a bare segfault into a detailed heap overflow report with a stack trace, saving hours of root-cause work. Parallel instances and Honggfuzz are also demonstrated.

The closing advice is that crashes may take days or weeks because fuzzing depends on randomness, so target one program at a time. Writing your own fuzzer can surface bugs that public tools miss, and a fuzzer that finds nothing does not prove the code is secure.

talks.title: Charting career paths in Cybersecurity | Bishakha Jain | Nullcon Webinar 2021
talks.teaser: Maps out varied cybersecurity career routes, the skills that matter, and practical ways to start learning.
talks.summary:
The session opens with a host introducing Bishakha Jain, an information security evangelist who works with women-in-security communities. The talk asks why cybersecurity matters and how someone can build a career in it, whether or not they start with a technical background. Bishakha begins with her own path: she started as a penetration tester, found she was more drawn to the audit, reporting and managerial side, completed an MBA focused on cybersecurity, and then moved into evangelism and awareness work.

The middle of the talk covers the skills she considers most useful. She points to analytical and mathematical thinking, a working grasp of programming, communication, teamwork and problem solving, and also stresses curiosity, integrity and resilience, including the willingness to unlearn outdated methods. She addresses common myths, arguing that a degree, a high IQ, a certification or a GitHub repository is not required to become a good practitioner. For newcomers she suggests finding a mentor, joining free workshops, following blogs, research papers and video channels, and trying capture-the-flag events and hackathons, while pairing hands-on practice with conceptual knowledge.

In the question session, she answers a question about the OSCP course by saying a certification makes sense when it serves a clear goal or job requirement, and that people should not spend their own money on credentials for their own sake. She closes by stressing continuous learning and that every role, from report writer to researcher to marketer, contributes to safer internet use.

talks.title: Migrate Securely from On Prem to Azure Cloud | Aditya Vasekar | Nullcon Webinar 2021
talks.teaser: Walks through planning, security controls and migration tooling for moving on-premises systems to Azure cloud.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by asking whether an organisation should move to the cloud at all. Reasons to hold back include strict compliance and data-location rules, proprietary software that may not suit cloud platforms, unreliable connectivity for remote sites, downtime risk and tight budgets. Before any migration, the speaker argues that goals and return on investment must be clear, since idle cloud resources can cost more than on-premises hardware.

Next, the talk covers the appeal of Azure, such as integrated services, DevOps tooling and broad compliance certifications, along with common migration models: lift and shift, moving to SaaS and restructuring applications. Common failures include missing security requirements, weak architecture, and a proof of concept run on production data that produced a bill of around 60 to 70 thousand dollars. Misconfigurations such as exposed APIs, open ports and default credentials are also covered. Mitigations discussed include centralised logging, network segmentation with NSGs and ASGs, and Azure Migrate and related assessment utilities that report on servers, SQL databases and web applications.

The final section covers identity and governance: flagging and monitoring admin accounts, reviewing user access, controlling emergency access to Active Directory, automating entitlements, and using Security Center and Sentinel for alerts and response. Case examples from Shopify, Spotify, Evernote, Boeing and BMW illustrate different migration motives, from scalability to analytics. The takeaway is that requirements, documentation and monitoring need planning before any data moves.
