talks.teaser: A keynote recounts decades of hands-on security work from early media duping and Apache SSL to bunker ops and silicon extraction.
talks.summary:
The session opens as an informal nullcon keynote whose title began as a dinner-table pun and never promised predictions or lottery numbers. Instead it situates the speaker in long-running hacker conference culture, from early DEF CON attendance and pseudonymous participation through years of staff work that now includes large-scale conference logistics, while arguing that vendors and governments in newer regions repeat the same slow acceptance of legitimate security research that the West eventually embraced.

The middle is a chronological memoir of practical tinkering: incompatible PC media and mass floppy production, CD layout experiments and writable-disc durability tests, a one-bit driver change that enabled raw audio ripping, and pushing back on inflated switch and jukebox specs during a rushed multichannel satellite audio build. It moves into distributing one of the first Apache SSL modules amid cryptography export rules, early online banking and telco engagements, and hosting from a refurbished underground bunker where exposure to the public internet brought immediate attacks and a turn toward offensive hardware work.

The close focuses on embedded targets: x-raying multi-die packages, drilling to bond wires with fuming nitric acid, capturing plaintext EEPROM traffic to recover keys, and reading masked ROM into disassemblable firmware. A short audience question affirms that bond-wire tapping remains widely applicable. The implied takeaway is to verify vendor claims by inspecting real behavior and to treat opaque hardware as fertile ground for the same skepticism applied to software decades earlier.

talks.title: A Hacker Walks Into A Co-Working Space | Rahul Binjve (@c0dist) | nullcon Goa 2019
talks.teaser: Visits to Pune co-working spaces reveal lax physical access, flat LANs, stale Wi-Fi secrets, and easy social tricks startups rarely address.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames shared offices as low-barrier targets for curious security-minded visitors: high churn of faces, cheap hot-desk rates, and little tenant control over door systems or guards’ habits. The speaker recounts field work across roughly ten venues in Pune, grouped into physical access, wired networking, Wi‑Fi, and social engineering, stressing that findings stay basic yet routinely exploitable without advanced tooling.

Physical anecdotes include bypassing reception via service lifts, propped-open server rooms beside tenant units, door controllers reachable on the LAN with default credentials, meeting-room passwords on pamphlets, and SSIDs or roadmap details written on glass walls. Network sections describe flat or poorly segmented VLANs, missing or misconfigured perimeter gear, exposed admin interfaces on Cyberoam-style firewalls, and neighbor-visible Windows Server 2008 and Shellshock-class hosts on shared switches. Wi‑Fi receives separate treatment: long-lived passwords, weak captive portals, router defaults, PPPoE secrets tied to ISP portals, and an SSID literally naming a server room that accepted admin logins.

Social angles cover chatty lunch crowds, housekeeping cards with access to every unit, and open cafe culture among unrelated companies. Closing material cites industry scale figures, warns that startup ideas and internal apps sit on these shared surfaces, and offers practical mitigations such as VPN use, segmented edge devices, employee awareness, and discreet SSIDs.

talks.title: Getting to $10,000 - the variables at play in determining bounty awards by Jarek Stanley
talks.teaser: Shows how report quality and impact shape Microsoft bounty payouts, with sample reports and recent program changes.
talks.summary:
Jarek Stanley, who leads the Microsoft Security Research Center's bounty work, explains how researchers can earn larger awards from the Microsoft bounty program. He outlines the scope, which spans Windows, Office and cloud services, with top awards running from tens of thousands of dollars up to 250,000 dollars for Hyper-V. Impact sets the reward tier: the STRIDE model is used to classify issues, and remote code execution sits in a higher tier than lower-severity bugs. Report quality is the second lever. Using low, medium and high quality sample reports, he shows that a report the team can reproduce, with clear steps and version or configuration details, earns more than a vague one. In one elevation of privilege example, a low-quality report would earn 1,000 dollars, clear reproduction steps raised it to 2,000 dollars, and added attack vectors, root cause analysis and patterns in other products raised it to 5,000 dollars.

He then covers recent changes. Top awards were raised in Windows, cloud and Azure DevOps, and researchers can now get an assessment and an award once a bug is reproduced, without waiting for a fix. Externally found duplicates of bugs Microsoft already knew about can still be paid. His closing advice is to focus on in-scope, high-priority targets, read the bounty brief, state assumptions about the test setup, and write up the attacker's perspective in a structured form.

talks.title: Interview with Robert Baptiste aka Elliot Alderson [@fs0c131y] by Antriksh Shah | nullcon Goa 2019
talks.teaser: Follows a French researcher's account of finding flaws in Indian government apps and the struggle to get them disclosed.
talks.summary:
The French independent researcher describes how he began examining official Indian applications in 2018, after followers asked him to look at the official Android app. The vulnerabilities he reported in that app, along with issues in government websites and a demo application tied to the Prime Minister, drew wide media attention and a large Indian following. He explains his interest in India as a matter of scale, since a system used by a very large population makes its security especially worth studying.

The middle of the conversation covers the hard parts of disclosure. Reaching the right person at an organization is often the biggest obstacle, though the technical staff he spoke to were usually cooperative. He described a data exposure caused by a third party storing sensitive records in an open directory, and a company that stayed silent for days until he published, then fixed the problem within hours. An audience member asked whether NCIPC could bridge the gap; an agency representative asked for patience, and he replied that attackers do not follow such processes.

The takeaway he stresses is that organizations should provide researchers with an email address and a secure channel, listen to reports, and act quickly when personal data is exposed. Researchers, in turn, should reach the right contact and protect user data while they communicate. The session closed with NCIPC pointing researchers to its vulnerability disclosure email address, and the interviewee saying he wanted an ongoing, direct exchange with the agency.

talks.summary:
### Overview
In this nullcon interview, George Eapen discusses his role as Global CISO and Head of Cybersecurity for Petrofac, an $8 billion London-headquartered multinational in the oil and gas sector employing close to 12,000 people. He outlines the primary responsibilities of a CISO—protecting the organization against external threats and insider risks while maintaining regulatory compliance—and explains how these priorities shift fundamentally between traditional sectors such as banking and the oil and gas industry.

### Key Topics
- **Role of the CISO Across Industries**: While the core mission of guarding against internal/external threats and ensuring compliance remains constant, the critical assets vary. Banking CISOs focus heavily on data confidentiality, customer-facing applications, and IT system availability, whereas oil and gas focuses on industrial operations and harsh physical environments.
- **Operational Technology (OT) Environments**: Managing cybersecurity across onshore and offshore sites presents distinct challenges compared to standard enterprise IT, largely because these environments rely on legacy, operational systems.
- **Workforce Awareness and Cyber Discipline**: Employees serve as both the first line of defense and the first point of failure. Fostering a company-wide cyber culture through training ensures field personnel understand appropriate operational actions, such as handling USB drives safely around older systems.
- **Prevent, Detect, and Respond**: Traditional security strategies heavily prioritize prevention, but organizations must balance investment across prevention, detection, and response as the threat landscape and technological solutions evolve.

### Technical Details
- **Compensating Perimeter Controls**: Because operational technology systems deployed on rigs and production sites are often legacy and difficult to replace or modify directly, organizations implement compensating security controls around the perimeter to protect critical infrastructure.
- **Removable Media Handling**: In OT settings where legacy systems are common, physical media such as USB drives are frequently required for operational tasks. Security training focuses on instructing staff on proper boundaries and safe handling when interacting with these sensitive systems.

### Takeaways
- Cybersecurity cannot rely solely on a dedicated security team; every employee must maintain baseline cyber discipline and awareness.
- Securing legacy OT in challenging onshore and offshore environments requires strong perimeter compensating controls coupled with human-layer defenses.
- Security strategies must balance investment across prevent, detect, and respond capabilities rather than relying exclusively on upfront prevention.

talks.teaser: Walks through building a hardware testing lab, from logic analyzers and flash readers to SDR radios for IoT devices.
talks.summary:
The talk is a practical guide to building a lab for testing IoT hardware. The speaker argues that a device cannot be judged alone, since its firmware, cloud service and companion app all shape its risk. Examples included firmware stored on external flash that could be read after the chip was removed, a doorbell whose RAM could be dumped through an exposed JTAG port to recover tokens, a microcontroller whose firmware could be dumped even with debugging disabled, and a smart switch sharing one hardcoded key across a vendor's devices. Wireless cases covered unencrypted packets that could be replayed.

Because hardware has no common standard, the speaker said no single kit fits every device. Advice was to buy for one project at a time and to get at least two units of a target. Wired tools mentioned were logic analyzers, oscilloscopes for side-channel or fault-injection work, FTDI-based adapters and Bus Pirate for SPI, I2C, JTAG and SWD, and a J-Link debugger. For radio, RTL-SDR only receives, while HackRF can transmit and receive, with USRP at the high end.

Rough budgets ranged from about 100 to 200 dollars for beginners to around 1,000 to 2,000 dollars for a moderate lab. The closing advice was to keep an ESD-safe workspace, work patiently, and keep hardware and software testers in close communication.

talks.title: Goa 2018:- Expanding Exploitation Beyond X86 And ARM
talks.teaser: Shows how return-oriented and jump-oriented exploitation work on Xtensa-based ESP32 chips with register windowing.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at exploitation beyond the usual x86 and ARM targets, focusing on small low-power IoT chips such as the ESP32 and ESP8266. The speakers explain that embedded operating systems often lack address space layout randomization, and that the Xtensa architecture separates instruction and data memory, which already blocks simple code injection on the stack.

The central difference is register windowing. Each function call rotates a window over a bank of physical registers and there are no push or pop instructions, so classic return-oriented gadgets that rely on the stack and on returns are hard to build. Jump-oriented programming avoids returns and therefore does not trigger the window rotation. The ESP8266 is easier to work with because usable gadgets are plentiful, including in boot ROM. A basic buffer overflow demo showed that physical registers must be exhausted before the window underflow handler can be abused. Debugging on real hardware used JTAG, OpenOCD and GDB, with a single core recommended for stepping.

The speakers said that gadget searching for the ESP32 was still in progress, with only partial sets found so far, and they plan to continue the work in future talks. A practitioner should take away that these devices have few exploit mitigations, that secure boot can stop persistent infection, and that inexpensive development boards make the platform easy to study.

talks.title: Goa 2018:- Keynote by Haroon Meer
talks.teaser: Urges security practitioners to chase important problems, build defensive tools, and pursue independent research over distraction.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In his keynote address at Nullcon Goa 2018, Haroon Meer (founder of Thinkst and creator of Thinkst Canary) reflects on his career across offensive security, defensive engineering, and product development. Drawing heavily on Richard Hamming’s classic essay and talk *You and Your Research*, as well as observations from Dan Geer and Brian Snow, Meer delivers advice directed at both young and experienced security professionals. He challenges the cybersecurity community to stop chasing passive distractions and instead tackle significant, enduring problems, urging practitioners—particularly offensive researchers—to embrace blue-team defense and product development.

### Key Topics
- **Distractions in InfoSec and Passive Learning:** The security industry is easily distracted by constant novelty and conference culture, which can turn into passive entertainment ("potato chips for your mind") rather than active learning and substantive problem-solving. Meer notes that aiming simply to be a conference speaker is an empty pursuit.
- **The Current Stagnation of Defense:** Despite millions spent, typical enterprise defense remains fragile. Meer references two heuristics: lateral movement in many organizations remains as easy as it was in 2003, and most organizations are only zero to one 0-days away from catastrophe.
- **Shifting from Red Team to Blue Team:** Breaking into networks has become relatively routine, and offensive techniques like social engineering are often overly easy rather than challenging. In contrast, defensive problems (such as local admin passwords or two-factor authentication) offer massive research opportunities and commercial potential (e.g., Duo Security).
- **Avoiding Utopian Thinking:** Defenders frequently let perfection undermine practical effectiveness. Meer cites EMET bypasses and the historical demise of the Linux honeypot tool Sebek (killed because researchers proved it could be detected via kernel syscall timing in a lab, despite attackers in the wild never performing such checks). Blue teams should "embrace the hack" and solve real-world organizational challenges rather than rejecting imperfect tools.
- **Hamming's Lessons on First-Class Research:** Success in groundbreaking work is rarely just luck. Key factors include independent thoughts, the courage to chase them, deep drive, and emotional commitment. Knowledge compounds like interest, meaning sustained extra effort leads to dramatically outsized productivity.

### Technical Details
- **Sebek and Honeypots:** Meer highlights Sebek, an early 2000s Honeynet Project rootkit-like tool designed to capture keystrokes and traffic from compromised boxes. Academic/lab demonstrations showed Sebek could be detected via precise syscall timing, leading defenders to shelve a tool that was otherwise effective against real-world adversaries who do not perform syscall timing.
- **Defensive Tooling and Pragmatism:** Mentioning Microsoft's Enhanced Mitigation Experience Toolkit (EMET), Meer illustrates that even if reverse engineers can bypass an exploit mitigation tool, deploying it still protects enterprises against common threats.
- **Compounding Work and Metasploit:** Meer uses HD Moore's creation of Metasploit as an example of restructuring ad-hoc work (copy-pasting shellcode and one-off exploits) into an open platform that others can build upon.
- **Thinkst Canary:** During the Q&A, Meer explains that Canary focuses on alerting organizations to compromises with minimal effort and low false positives, addressing the organizational challenge of adoption rather than merely writing technical code.

### Takeaways
- **Dedicate Time to Great Thoughts:** Regularly schedule time to ask yourself: "What are the important problems in your field, and why aren't you working on them?"
- **Embrace Constraints and Put in the Work:** First-class research requires intense dedication and emotional investment rather than relying on talent, luck, or ideal working conditions.
- **Focus on Usable Solutions:** Tackle enterprise organizational barriers directly rather than blaming users or abandoning tools over minor edge cases. High-value opportunities exist in building resilient, usable defensive products.

Turning to the wider field, the interviewee argues that digitization and new technology keep widening the attack surface, so organizations that once had confined architectures are now more open and exposed. In their view, relying on processes and audits alone will not keep pace with that change, and defenders need deep technical expertise. They also point to policy, privacy and data protection questions raised by technology as major concerns worldwide.

The takeaway is that security teams should pair compliance work with hands-on technical depth, and that events bringing technical specialists together with policy perspectives help practitioners keep up with fast-moving threats.

talks.summary:
This short clip introduces a hardware-focused capture-the-flag contest held at the Nullcon conference in Goa in 2018. Phillip Ingram explains that, unlike the software-based CTFs elsewhere at the event, every challenge here requires physical hardware, and the organisers supply the tools and the challenges so participants do not need to bring their own equipment.

The challenge types described include RFID tasks, where a door reader must be opened by cloning or faking a card, and tasks where players sniff the exchange between a phone and a card to recover a flag. Other challenges involve tapping communication lines on circuit boards. Because those lines are often hard to reach on real devices, a micro-soldering challenge asks players to expose PCB tracks and solder very thin wires onto them. talks.title: Goa 2018:- Comprehensive Hacker Techniques in Mobile Networks
talks.teaser: Shows how SS7 signaling flaws let attackers bypass SMS routing, track subscriber locations and intercept one-time passwords.
talks.summary:
Chris Janko presents research from security monitoring and assessment work done for mobile operators. He explains that SS7, the signaling protocol behind mobile networks, was designed in the 1970s on the assumption of a closed network, and that its weaknesses carried over when it moved onto IP-based SIGTRAN. Because roaming interconnects trust traffic from other operators, anyone with access to one network can reach subscribers on another. He recalls a 2017 case where this kind of access was used to intercept one-time passwords and move money.

The middle of the talk covers three bypass techniques. The first abuses SMS home routing: a crafted send-routing-info request built on an IMSI-style numbering plan skips the SMS router and returns the real IMSI and serving switch address. The second is position refinement, where provide-subscriber queries and a malformed unstructured notify message make base stations report several cell IDs, narrowing where a subscriber is. The third is a firewall bypass, where spoofed update-location messages pass the velocity check because only the home country code is compared.

The closing advice is to correct routing tables so SMS queries reach the SMS router, block the message category used for location queries, and check both VLR and MSC addresses in update-location messages. The speaker stresses that ongoing assessment, vulnerability management and monitoring matter more than any single tool.

talks.title: Goa 2018:- Looting your bank savings using Digital India
talks.teaser: Maps several patched weaknesses in India's digital banking stack, from passbook kiosks and wallets to OTP checks and Aadhaar KYC.
talks.summary:
After India's 2016 demonetization push toward cashless payments, millions of new bank accounts and self-service passbook printers appeared nationwide. The speaker—a computer science student presenting research—states upfront that every issue covered has since been fixed or reported, and that some material was removed for legal reasons after recent banking scandals.

The walkthrough begins with passbook printing machines that authenticated users solely via barcodes, often encoding public account numbers, allowing balance details to be retrieved with a spoofed barcode; a small tool helps identify vulnerable banks, generate account numbers, and produce barcodes. Later segments cover authentication bypasses in state government wallet apps linked to bank transfers, early BHIM problems such as self-payment loops and revealing registered names from phone numbers, and an SBI online transfer flaw where changing an OTP-related request flag sent payments without valid codes. A branch "forgot password" workflow leaks prefilled customer data when PDF reference numbers are incremented. The closing thread explains Aadhaar e-KYC architecture (AUAs versus sub-AUAs) and a bypass that could validate demographic data while attribution landed on another agency—combinable with earlier leaks for convincing fraud.

Practitioners should treat the talk as a lesson that rushed digitization and single-factor checks created high-impact, low-complexity risks, and that chaining balance disclosure, identity verification, and contact data magnifies social engineering—not as a guide to active exploitation.

talks.title: Goa 2018:- I Boot when U-Boot
talks.teaser: Demonstrates a U-Boot bootkit that persists below the firmware on embedded routers and survives updates and factory resets.
talks.summary:
The talk presents a bootkit for embedded devices that run U-Boot, a bootloader common in routers and other IoT hardware. The speaker explains why the bootloader is an attractive place for persistence: it starts before the operating system, is rarely touched by firmware updates and can survive factory resets. The main risk is that a mistake can leave a device unusable, which makes the work highly device-specific.

The research targeted an open-source OpenWrt router. The team dumped the flash chip for backups, built MIPS binaries with a cross-compilation toolchain from the OpenWrt SDK, and edited U-Boot environment variables and the boot command. The boot command was changed to check whether a command-and-control host answers a ping, and if it does, to fetch a backdoored kernel over TFTP. Other changes hid the backdoor variables from printenv and made a key press at the bootloader prompt wipe the flash. A kernel module was described that clears the read-only flags on MTD partitions so the bootloader partition can be written from Linux.

For defence, the speaker suggested reproducible U-Boot builds, with hashes of data sections compared against known-good images, and cryptographic signing as used in secure boot. He noted that secure boot can be defeated when no key is present or through a TFTP overflow, and that hardware write protection, as on some Chromebooks, adds a physical barrier. The conclusion was that device security needs physical protections, firmware transparency and better bootloader analysis tools.

talks.title: Goa 2018:- A Game between Adversary and AI Scientist
talks.teaser: Shows how deception decoys and machine learning reveal an intruder's moves during a simulated attack.
talks.summary:
The talk casts intrusion response as a game between an adversary and a defender. It argues that attackers operate in a vast, open state space while defenders often lack visibility once someone is inside the network. The speaker proposes bounding that space with the MITRE ATT&CK matrix and gaining visibility through two tools: deception and AI.

The demos follow one intruder. After a port scan finds an open RDP port on a sales host, the defender gets an alert, spins up high-interaction decoys and plants credentials in that network segment. In a second scenario the attacker logs in over RDP, runs an obfuscated PowerShell command built with an obfuscation tool, loads PowerSploit modules, dumps credentials and exfiltrates them over a DNS tunnel. Raw logs in the thousands are condensed to a few tens of notable actions by filtering a baseline and applying domain rules with NLP. Classifiers trained on public PowerShell scripts flag obfuscation, and a model trained on DNS sequences flags the tunnel and its domain.

The speaker models the exchange as a simple normal-form game with payoffs for each side. In the Q&A, the speaker said the training data came from open-source scripts and that a deception alert was the detection source. The closing message is that deception plus AI can give defenders visibility, and that fusing security tooling with AI remains an open problem.

talks.teaser: A panel weighs cyber risk in connected manufacturing, cloud services, oil and gas SCADA, and global compliance programs.
talks.summary:
The session opens by tracing how communications and industrial operations evolved from early mechanization through microcontrollers to Industry 4.0, where Wi-Fi, cellular, cloud, and analytics knit factories, vehicles, and homes into one connected stack. The moderator sets out to catalogue the digital risks security practitioners must recognize and how organizations can respond when every new link in that stack widens exposure.

Kabir Mulchandani describes Synopsys shifting from siloed chip design to highly automated supply chains, building a software integrity practice, and tackling heterogeneous environments through architectural risk analysis, supplier diligence, evidence of testing, and DevSecOps rather than late-stage bolt-ons. He stresses that compliance alone does not equal security. Ram from Genpact explains rapid digital and cloud growth, acquisition integration, robotic process risks, and why disciplined process and partnerships matter as much as tooling. Sudarshan Rajagopal outlines Shell's physical-digital span from extraction and floating assets through refineries and retail, blending drones, bots, new platforms, and legacy SCADA while pursuing correlation and staged consolidation. Vijay Patel Swamy frames global compliance as an escalating obligation that only works through collaborative, geography-aware risk assessment that enables product teams.

The panel links physical safety to security in automotive and medical devices, discusses how threat focus shifts across confidentiality, availability, and integrity, and debates talent, education, and partner hygiene in India's market. Questions from the floor target legacy Windows-based ICS in heavy industry and secure paths from on-premises systems to cloud. The closing emphasizes people, process, and technology, thorough architecture reviews, safety as a driver for investment, and long-term competency.

talks.teaser: Panelists from banking, shipping, and payments discuss insider threats, endpoints, analytics, and threat intelligence for CISOs.
talks.summary:
The session frames cybersecurity leadership as adapting industry standards to real organizations rather than treating checklists as copy-paste mandates. The moderator structures discussion around four breach surfaces: malicious insiders, stolen credentials, compromised endpoints, and vulnerable applications, with three CISO-level panelists from UAE banking, diversified Indian industry, and global payments.

On insider risk, one panelist stresses governance and influence over pure technology, arguing collusion in high-value authorization chains cannot be fully solved by tools alone, while another describes processing on the order of eight billion security events daily, using machine learning funnels and analyst feedback to label anomalies and shrink noise. A third explains partnering with business units to define deviation baselines for SOC alerting. Endpoint protection in remote plants includes rolling out complementary signatureless memory-scrambling controls with quarantine for noncompliance. Analytics coverage spans patching visibility, control posture on privileged workstations, and aspirations for dynamic routing of attacks to the right controls.

Threat intelligence discussion covers vendor evaluation, normalization and orchestration of indicators, bank peer sharing, and practical peer networks beyond formal feeds. Closing themes emphasize continuous incident-response readiness, identity-based outlier detection limits before compromise, red-team validation, and layered fail-safe design when patches lag disclosure.

talks.title: Goa 2018:- Should all CISO promote Hall of Fame within their organizations?
talks.teaser: Panelists debate whether CISOs should run hall of fame recognition and bug bounty programs, and how maturity shapes that choice.
talks.summary:
The panel asked whether chief information security officers should promote hall of fame recognition and bug bounty programs inside their organisations. The moderator first polled the audience on CTF and bounty experience, and an attendee from Adobe described running both a hall of fame and a private bounty program. Speakers largely tied the choice to organisational maturity. Several argued that a hall of fame suits an early-stage company, while a paid bounty needs solid security investment and steady engagement with researchers.

Risks dominated much of the exchange. One panelist said a poorly managed bounty can cause reputational damage, pointing to reports left unanswered for months, which push researchers to go public. Another recounted a researcher who demanded a reply within 12 hours and turned out to have sent similar messages to many others. An open-source vendor said a public bounty adds little when its code is already open to review, while a speaker from a government context noted that closed environments make bounties more useful. Internal bounties drew mixed reactions, with some seeing value in employees spotting business-process flaws and others warning about insider access and morale.

The panel also touched on SOC effectiveness, suggesting bounty findings could show whether alerts fire during testing, and on threat intelligence, where partial disclosures might signal wider risk. The moderator closed by summarising the main themes: recognition versus cash, the need to keep programs responsive, and the importance of matching the model to the organisation's stage.

talks.title: 2017 - Invoke Obfuscation: Powershell Obfuscation Techniques n How To Try To Detect Them
talks.teaser: Shows how PowerShell obfuscation slips past keyword-based detections, and how defenders can hunt for obfuscation itself.
talks.summary:
The talk covers PowerShell obfuscation from both red and blue team sides, presented by an incident response consultant who built the Invoke-Obfuscation tool. Its core argument is that detections based on exact command-line strings are fragile, because PowerShell accepts many equivalent spellings. Using a remote download cradle as the example, the speaker shows how each element can change: implied prefixes can be dropped, escape characters inserted, strings split and rebuilt, and command aliases or other download methods substituted.

The middle section groups the techniques into layers. Token-level tricks change how commands, arguments and members appear. String-level tricks reverse, split or replace text before it is evaluated. Encoding options include secure strings tied to a key and abbreviated flag variants. Launch tricks move the arguments into parent or grandparent processes, standard input, environment variables or the clipboard, so the process command line may look harmless. The speaker notes that script block logging keeps some token-level artifacts.

The closing advice is to enable process command-line logging, such as event 4688 or Sysmon, and PowerShell 5 module and script block logging with larger log sizes. Defenders should go beyond listing known bad syntax and hunt for signs of obfuscation, such as unusual character counts or frequencies. A live demo of version 1.8 showed the tool's menus, random syntax selection and process argument trees for launchers.

talks.title: Goa 2017 - Barbarians At The Gateway by Dave Lewis
talks.teaser: Platform telemetry maps volumetric and web attacks, criminal DDoS tooling, and hygiene steps defenders can apply from raw data.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by arguing that security narratives should rest on raw telemetry instead of fear-driven media hype, framed through decades of practitioner experience and published case material. It then walks through the attacker landscape: underground for-hire menus, bored teenagers recruited as disposable labor, activist chaos, and groups such as the Al-Qassam Cyber Fighters targeting financial sites with announced distributed denial-of-service campaigns.

The middle of the talk is data-heavy. HTTP application flaws—SQL injection, local file inclusion, and cross-site scripting—dominate observed web attacks across multiple quarters. Volumetric abuse leans on misconfigured reflectors including NTP, SSDP, SNMP, and DNS, with quarter-over-quarter growth in attack density. Retail and travel absorb more traffic than hardened banks. Extortion actors such as DD4BC and copycats demanded modest Bitcoin ransoms; commoditized booters and stressors lower the bar further. Mirai and default IoT credentials, HOIC variants, WordPress-based botnets, and simple HTTP flood tools illustrate how cheap tooling scales impact.

The close stresses defender actions: sanitize inputs and outputs, patch daemons and routers, avoid single-provider DNS, resist credential reuse after breaches, and evaluate vendors through bake-offs rather than hype. Observational platform statistics are pointed to at stateoftheinternet.com, with a tribute to Howard Schmidt woven in before Q&A on stressor hosting and open-source security debt.

talks.title: Goa 2017 - Increasing Your Impact On Facebook Bug Bounty by Jack Whitton
talks.teaser: Explains how to make Facebook bug bounty reports more impactful and avoid common false positives.
talks.summary:
The talk gives practical advice for getting Facebook bug bounty reports triaged faster and with more impact. It starts with the program's scope, which covered Facebook apps, Instagram, WhatsApp, HHVM and React, and with its scale: over 100 reports a day, more than $5 million paid to 900-plus researchers, and a top payout of $335,000 for a code execution bug in OpenID. The speaker, from Facebook's product security team, recommends retesting in incognito mode with fresh accounts to rule out cookie or cache side effects, and including user IDs, content IDs and full URLs in reports.

The middle section covers common false positives that flood the queue. Accepting several variations of a password at login is a deliberate usability choice, rate limits may simply have thresholds the tester has not reached, and marketing micro-sites on separate infrastructure hold no user data, so a missing X-Frame-Options header there is usually low impact.

The closing examples are 2016 reports with real impact: a GraphQL mutation that let one page's messaging setting be changed without a permission check, an email address exposed through hidden markup in the page admin invite flow, video attachments that could be used to delete other users' comments, and an insecure direct object reference in Business Manager that allowed claiming another user's page. The speaker suggests targeting new features, reading engineering blogs, checking mobile and m. subdomains, and inspecting raw HTTP responses for data hidden in the interface.

talks.title: Goa 2017 - DevOpSec: Rapid Security In The AWS Cloud by Mikhail Advani and Rajesh Tamhane
talks.teaser: Shows how to run an open-source set of AWS security checks inside a CI pipeline to catch exposed ports and policy gaps early.
talks.summary:
Mikhail Advani opens by describing DevOps as a practice where development, operations and security are not split into separate teams, so each person shares all three roles and security decisions happen early. He presents a small open-source test suite for AWS accounts, built after a data center to cloud migration of about 125 servers for a consumer electronics client. Its checks draw on the CIS AWS Foundations benchmark, AWS guidance and field experience. The suite is a Python script using the AWS SDK with 16 tests that can be enabled or disabled, and he says he runs it on a personal account for about two dollars a month.

In a live demo, the suite runs from a Go CD pipeline and covers IAM policies, CloudTrail monitoring and logging, and whether SSH or RDP is open to the public internet. The network check reviews security group rules for port 3389 and for open TCP or all-traffic rules. An RDP test failed, the security group was corrected, and a rerun passed. The run takes about 30 seconds and only queries the AWS API. He calls the suite detective and corrective rather than preventive, and suggests running it on every infrastructure change, plus periodically for governance items such as credential rotation, since AWS regenerates its credentials report about every four hours.

In the Q&A he compares it with Netflix's Security Monkey, which has far wider coverage, and suggests native cloud monitoring such as CloudWatch for continuous checks. Findings belong to the team that owns the infrastructure code. His closing takeaways are that teams moving from legacy data centers often copy old firewall rules, even though the cloud is reached over the public internet; that version-controlled infrastructure automation makes rollback easier; and that service secrets need a plan from the start, such as a key or secrets manager.

talks.title: Goa 2017 - Engineering Better Security At Facebook by Karen Sittig
talks.teaser: Shows how Facebook builds security checks into PHP tooling, code review, fuzzing and certificate monitoring.
talks.summary:
Karen Sittig, a software engineer on Facebook's detection and security infrastructure team, explains how the company builds security into its development process. With a small security staff and code pushed several times a day, the team writes developer tools that make secure code the default.

She walks through four stages of the lifecycle. For writing code, she covers Hack, a compiled PHP dialect running on HHVM, whose type checker catches mistakes such as a missing await on an asynchronous call. Its XHP library escapes output automatically, which she says nearly eliminated cross-site scripting on the platform. For review, she describes Phabricator and Arcanist, with lint checks before a change is posted and Herald rules that subscribe reviewers or flag deprecated patterns, like a raw MySQL query call instead of an internal database API. For code in production, she recommends fuzzers such as AFL, run where permissions change or input is collected, and cites a PHP string deserialization crash that fuzzing turned up.

Last, she demonstrates the Certificate Transparency monitoring tool, which lets domain owners get alerts when a certificate is issued for their site, helping catch impersonation. Her takeaway is that tools built into everyday workflows let developers and security teams both work better, and that the ones she covered are open source.

talks.title: Goa 2017 - Bug Bounty Reports: How Do They Work by Adam Bacchus
talks.teaser: Shows how to write bug bounty reports that security teams can triage quickly, using good and bad real-world examples.
talks.summary:
Adam Bacchus, chief bounty officer at HackerOne, explains how to write bug bounty reports that a security team can act on. He defines core terms such as vulnerability, report, disclosure and bounty program, and stresses that the internal security team is the real audience, since it must persuade developers to fix a bug. Scope comes next: he explains why some assets are excluded and why a hunter should ask about anything unlisted. He also covers service level expectations, including first response, bounty decisions and remediation timelines by severity.

The middle section focuses on report content. A strong report includes reproduction steps, a realistic account of exploitability, and an impact statement tied to confidentiality, integrity and availability for the organization's assets. Bacchus contrasts a clickjacking report with a working proof-of-concept page against a bare claim that a server runs outdated software, and notes that low-severity issues like open redirects or logout CSRF rarely merit a report unless chained with something else. Real examples show how clarity and tone shape outcomes, from a password-change flaw that was easy to reproduce to a researcher whose hostile replies ended their participation on the platform.

He closes with advice on handling disagreements, such as explaining why a report is out of scope or marking duplicates with timestamps, and on public disclosure after a fix. Resources include the Web Application Hacker's Handbook, Google Bug Hunter University, Google Gruyere and HackerOne's hacktivity feed of disclosed reports.

talks.title: Goa 2017 - Nearly Generic Fuzzing Of XML Based Formats by Nicholas Gregoire
talks.teaser: Explains how structure-aware mutation and reusable XML fragments help fuzz XSLT and SVG parsers, along with the bugs found that way.
talks.summary:
The talk covers fuzzing file formats built on XML, such as XSLT and SVG. Generating inputs from a grammar produces files that are valid but shallow, while random byte changes break the syntax, so neither reaches much of the code. The speaker builds on earlier XSLT feature research, which produced a corpus of stylesheets covering most of the language and is reused as seed material.

The mutation engine works at three levels. A generic structural layer parses the XML tree and adds, removes or replaces nodes and attributes, drawing replacements from fragments stored in a per-format SQLite database; the same removal logic also minimises crashing inputs. An optional dialect layer applies format-specific changes, such as enabling XSLT's forward-compatible mode or repairing variable references, which led to more use-after-free bugs. The bottom layer is byte-level mutation delegated to AFL, with the engine plugged in as an external Python mutator. Large applications run in persistent or in-process modes, with AddressSanitizer builds used for deeper checks.

After a few months of runs, the XSLT targets reached roughly a billion executions per day and an SVG target about nine million. Findings included a low-impact libxslt bug that needed a namespace from the earlier corpus, Adobe Reader bugs including two earlier issues that reappeared and two new use-after-free bugs, a Firefox use-after-free that was fixed with further reports pending, and an Inkscape crash that may allow control of the instruction pointer. The takeaway is that structure-aware mutation combined with a feature corpus reaches code that plain fuzzing misses. Planned next steps include more dialects, more targets and Windows support.

talks.title: Goa 2017 - Hacking Medical Devices And Infrastructure by Anirudh Duggal
talks.teaser: Walks through HL7 2.x hospital messaging, its common flaws, crash-style denial tests and a recon tool.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at HL7 2.x, the messaging standard that much of healthcare depends on to exchange clinical data between systems. The speaker explains the wire format, which wraps plain-text messages in framing bytes and header segments that use delimiters, and walks through the main message types. These cover admissions, orders, patient observations, pharmacy dispensing and billing, and the speaker shows how each one could expose or alter patient records.

The middle of the talk moves to testing. Captured hospital traffic is usually unencrypted, so it can be sniffed on the network, and the speaker reports systems that accept messages from unverified sources and do not enforce size limits. Nmap guesses poorly at the services these devices run, so the speaker introduces a custom auditor that scans ports, sends header probes and reads acknowledgements to map which message types a port accepts. Demonstrations included suppressing acknowledgements so a monitor keeps resending stale readings, oversized or repeated payloads that crash devices, and held connections that exhaust a server's threads.

The closing takeaways are practical: enforce encryption with mutual TLS, validate message size and sender identity, add checksums, and anonymize patient names in messages. The speaker also notes that FHIR, a JSON and REST-based successor, is spreading, and that older HL7 flaws are sometimes carried into it.

talks.title: Goa 2017 - Silicon: Security's New Layer by Joshua Pennell
talks.teaser: Covers chip-level attacks, backdoored silicon and hardware supply chain risk, told from a software engineer's point of view.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that software defenses have improved, so attackers are moving lower in the stack into hardware and embedded devices. It opens with past cases: a 2003 backdoor in the Linux source tree that differed by a single character, and a university paper describing how an insider at a chip foundry could add one extra cell to a mask, creating a backdoor that is very hard to detect.

The middle section covers supply chain trust and profit-driven hardware hacking. Examples include a 2005 memo telling agencies to stop buying certain Lenovo hardware over suspected backdoors, a claim that network gear was intercepted and re-taped in transit, a telecom that bought cheaper vendor kit and spent the savings on security audits, the satellite pay-TV smart card dispute between rival companies, and the Atari versus Nintendo lockout chip. The technical part walks through lab work: decapping packages, imaging dies under a microscope, focused ion beam edits to reroute signals, backside imaging, and power and clock glitching. It also notes that embedded devices often ship with default passwords, unauthenticated bootloaders, and debug ports that can dump firmware.

The closing advice is to map your supply chain, ask who vets people writing the code, and commission third-party tamper testing. Designers should remove exposed serial consoles, avoid hardcoded credentials, and encrypt memory and buses. Because patching silicon is costly, the speaker urges software teams to engage hardware people early. The Q&A touched on sourcing from distrusted countries, where trusted foundry programs and FIPS 140 or Common Criteria offer only partial assurance.

talks.title: Goa 2014:- Jailbreak
talks.teaser: A team recounts Jay Break at nullcon Goa: web flaws, product hunts, disclosures, and lessons from solving under time pressure.
talks.summary:
The session looks back at nullcon Goa 2014’s Jailbreak (Jay Break), a multi-day contest that mixed offensive security work with structured courses, coding tasks, and timed mini-challenges. The format drew on earlier Jay Break editions; teams had to move through jail-themed stages, break numbered courses, and hit task-specific goals while organisers kept tight clocks and bonus access for faster solves.

Presenters describe how their group prioritised reconnaissance on live targets: open CMS code review, injection and upload paths, distributor-user abuse, and product surfaces that should not have been exposed. They reported several findings across books, passports, and external-facing apps, and walked through a late push on a Google acquisitions-style task—hunting a “zero day” angle via product search, account password reset flows, and mobile verification pressure. Side threads mention bypassing open lists on other sites and coordinating writes-ups on contest infrastructure.

Closing segments cover how prizes were allocated—per-product findings, per-disclosure amounts, team awards, and judge observations favoring disciplined, methodical problem solving—and what participants gained from the environment: operating under fatigue, pairing creativity with basic approaches, and building relationships across the community.

talks.title: Goa 2015: Building custom scans for real world enterprise network by Sanoop Thomas
talks.teaser: Shows a graphical IDE that eases writing Nmap Scripting Engine scripts with autocomplete, templates and in-editor debugging.
talks.summary:
The speaker, an independent security researcher, starts from the Nmap Scripting Engine, which has grown to around 500 scripts for vulnerability checks, brute forcing and exploitation. These scripts are written in Lua, a lightweight language that needs no compilation. Writing them is slow, though: traditional editors offer little help, debugging means running Nmap from the command line, and library functions have to be looked up in online documentation again and again. Scripts also run conditionally, so one only fires when the scan finds a matching service such as FTP.

To address this, he built a free, Java-based development environment that recognises both Lua syntax and Nmap library functions. It offers autocomplete, debugging inside the editor, and settings for the local Nmap installation, script paths and word lists. He walks through creating a project from a generated skeleton, filling in the author, port, categories and license. For the example he builds a Shellshock check against a CGI script, places the payload in an HTTP User-Agent header, sends a GET request, and returns the status code and response to the scan output. He also notes that Nmap scripts now cover web checks such as SQL injection, so Nmap increasingly works as a web application scanner.

The practical takeaway is that custom Nmap scripts can be written quickly with editor support, instead of repeatedly checking documentation. The tool is free and runs on any operating system with a Java runtime. The speaker suggests that easier script writing could encourage more community contributions to Nmap.

talks.title: Goa 2015: Hacking Tizen The OS of Everything by Ajin Abraham
talks.teaser: Surveys Tizen's app model and security design, then presents research on its ASLR, CSP, and browser weaknesses.
talks.summary:
Tizen is presented as a Linux-based, open-source operating system aimed at smart home and many device types, not just phones. The talk covers its native C++ and web app formats, where apps are installed, and the web APIs that give web apps direct device access. It then outlines the security design: apps run as a non-root user, SMACK provides mandatory access control with a very large rule set, and web apps must define a content security policy.

The research section examines web apps, memory protection, and the WebKit-based browser. A demo showed shellcode placed on the stack of a native app still running, meaning non-executable stack protection was absent. The speaker also showed that address space randomization was ineffective in Tizen 2.2, since a changed process personality setting disabled it and library addresses repeated across launches. In the browser, a script opening a new window could write content into a tab labelled with a trusted domain, and a null-byte trick in a script URL bypassed a same-origin policy that Chrome enforced.

For testers, the talk suggests a methodology covering certificate and signature checks, manifest review for excess privileges, SMACK rules, C++ code review, emulator-based dynamic analysis, and decrypting traffic by installing a proxy certificate. The speaker concludes the design is ambitious but complex enough that developers may misconfigure it, and that the research is ongoing.

talks.title: Goa 2015: Anatomy of a credit card stealing POS malware by Amol Sarwate
talks.teaser: Walks through a homegrown RAM-scraping point-of-sale malware, showing how card data is pulled from memory and what defenders can do.
talks.summary:
The talk examines point-of-sale terminals and how payment card data can be taken from them. It begins with a 2014 Verizon breach report that put POS intrusions at the top for the accommodation sector, then explains how magnetic stripe tracks one and two store cardholder fields. The core problem is timing: card data sits unencrypted in memory for a very short window before the payment software encrypts it, so a scraper has to reach it first.

To demonstrate, the speaker wrote a homegrown RAM-scraping program instead of dissecting an existing malware family, so its source could be walked through. It locates the payment process by module name, enables the debug privilege for its own token, opens that process, and reads only committed, non-image memory. Regular expressions match track data, and the Luhn algorithm filters out invalid numbers. A live swipe on a terminal produced the card number, name and expiry date. A second attempt after the transaction completed found nothing, because the software had cleared those variables from memory.

The closing section covered mitigations. Terminal owners should use POS machines only for their intended purpose, lock down remote management, and guard against insider tampering. Vendors should encrypt card data quickly using built-in libraries rather than custom code. Devices with end-to-end encryption were presented as safer than cheap one-sided readers, and chip-and-pin was described as stronger than magnetic stripe, though the speaker noted that chip-and-pin had also been attacked in research.

talks.title: Goa 2015: Keynote by Dr. Paul Vixie
talks.teaser: Explains how DNS creates security problems and defenses, covering response rate limiting, DNS firewalls, and passive DNS forensics.
talks.summary:
Vixie opens by arguing that DNS sits beneath nearly everything online, so DNS traces often reveal how an intrusion happened. He gives a short primer on zones and name servers, and contrasts DNS, which attackers must keep truthful, with WHOIS records that can be hidden. He then covers TSIG for authenticating zone transfers and DNSSEC for signing zone contents, urging operators to sign zones and validate.

The middle section turns to DNS abuse. He explains spoofed-source reflection attacks, then presents response rate limiting, a lightweight method that lets an authoritative server stop answering repeated identical queries from one netblock. One operator saw query traffic of roughly 150 to 250 megabits drop after deploying it. He criticises incremental fixes that push spammers toward cheap, instantly registered domains, and describes DNS firewalls built on response policy zones that can block, redirect or fabricate answers. Passive DNS sensors that omit end-user addresses feed a database for historical and wildcard lookups in investigations.

In the question period he discussed rate limiting for resolvers facing amplification and questioned trust in certificate authorities, offering DANE as an alternative built on DNSSEC. His takeaways: enable rate limiting, consider response policy zones, and treat DNS records as forensic evidence.

talks.title: Goa 2015: ICS SCADA Security Analysis of a Beckhoff CX5020 PLC by Hans Hoefken
talks.teaser: Walks through a security assessment of an older Beckhoff CX5020 PLC and its exposed remote services and weak authentication.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a Beckhoff CX5020 programmable logic controller, an older embedded PC running Windows CE 6.0 inside an industrial control environment. The speaker contrasts SCADA priorities, where availability comes before integrity and confidentiality, and explains why older controllers stay in service for years. The device is managed through TwinCAT software and the ADS protocol, which relies on net IDs and sends credentials without encryption.

The assessment started with an Nmap scan of an unconfigured unit, which showed 16 open ports, including 987, 5120 and 48899; the last is a maintenance port listed on the vendor's website. Telnet was enabled by default with a known default account, and the built-in web server exposed a remote admin virtual directory that gave full control once a password was set. A ZMap survey run for three to four hours found more than 100 Beckhoff devices online. Brute forcing the ADS service on port 48899 reached about 8,000 passwords per second, and the PPTP VPN could be attacked after its handshake was captured. A USB Wi-Fi adapter with a built-in driver offered a route that could potentially bypass infrastructure firewalls.

The recommendations for suppliers are to disable the remote admin directory and Telnet, limit ADS packets per second to stop brute forcing, ship devices with strong passwords instead of defaults, remove the Wi-Fi drivers, and replace PPTP with another VPN technology. The overall message is that legacy controllers reachable from networks need hardening and careful firewall review.

talks.title: Goa 2015: Keynote by Katie Moussouris
talks.teaser: Explains how vulnerability coordination and bounty incentives fit secure development when organizations loop findings into their lifecycle.
talks.summary:
The keynote frames bug bounties as one piece of vulnerability coordination inside a security development lifecycle, not a cheap substitute for penetration testing or a way to skip building security in. It touches ISO work on disclosure front doors and meaningful advisories, then stresses organizational empathy: incentives should match what the business actually risks losing when security fails.

The core narrative walks through how Microsoft shaped several programs with explicit goals—early residual finding, researcher engagement, and market disruption beyond raw cash. Examples include six-figure awards for new mitigation bypass techniques and defense ideas, and a time-limited Internet Explorer 11 preview bounty that shifted report timing by paying during beta when bulletin credit had effectively closed the free market. Riot Games’ SDL artwork illustrates the same loop for a modern product team.

Closing guidance urges vendors to operationalize goals, measure whether reported issues grow harder over time, and feed coordination results back into the SDL. The talk ends on policy: broad anti-hacking laws can chill good-faith reporting even where organizations welcome disclosures, so builders should engage lawmakers on the value of ethical hacking.

talks.title: Goa 2015: The NSA Playset RF Retroreflectors by Michael Ossmann
talks.teaser: Shows how radar-illuminated RF retro-reflector implants can covertly capture keyboard, USB, and video signals.
talks.summary:
Michael Ossmann opens by framing active emission security as an under-researched area, contrasting it with passive Tempest-style monitoring. He recaps the Great Seal bug, a microphone and antenna hidden in a carving and revealed in 1960, which was illuminated by radar to pick up room audio. He then covers the NSA ANT catalog leaked in 2013, which lists retro-reflector implants such as a VGA video tap, a keystroke implant, a beacon, and an audio device. He stresses that his own designs are forward-engineered and only loosely inspired by those leaked documents.

The middle of the talk explains the technique: an attacker fires a radar signal at a tiny implant, which modulates the reflection with the signal on a target cable, and the attacker recovers that data from the return. He describes cheap radar options, including a toy radar gun with a baseband output, and his HackRF transceivers operating at 2482 MHz at very low power. He shows his own implants for PS2 and low-speed USB keyboards and for VGA, recovering a keystroke pattern and a screen image from the reflected signal. He notes that the keystroke demo was run from earlier captured data rather than live.

He closes by saying countermeasures are not yet well understood, since detection requires sweeping a wide range of frequencies and is hard to do well. He suggests that noise jamming could be defeated by correlating the transmitted noise with its reflection. He urges researchers to build and test these systems, and to respect spectrum rules and local laws.

talks.title: Goa 2015: Drone Attacks How I hijacked a drone by Rahul Sasi
talks.teaser: Shows how a consumer quadcopter's control firmware can be reversed and backdoored through a serial port proxy.
talks.summary:
Rahul Sasi opens by explaining why he started this research: drones are spreading into surveillance, delivery and other uses, and a blog post on drone malware drew wide attention. He wanted to answer whether a drone bought from another country could be backdoored, and how a security flaw in one could be found. He covers quadcopter basics, including how the control software relies on gyroscope, ultrasonic and pressure sensors to hover, stabilise and land.

The research targets a consumer Parrot AR Drone. Dynamic analysis was impractical because setting breakpoints stopped the motors, so he obtained the control binary, program.elf, from a firmware update and a telnet service on the device, then reversed it in IDA. Debug strings helped him map functions, and data section references revealed the serial ports linked to motors and sensors. He focused on the autonomous auto-landing routine and found it used raw sensor altitude readings without checking them against earlier values. In his toy demonstration, a nearby object spoofing the sensor made the drone shut its motors down.

For the malware part, he built a generic proof of concept called maldrone, written in Go, that sits between the control program and the hardware. It kills the original program, patches serial port references in the binary, and opens a reverse connection to an attacker, with a Python script used to upload it. The live demo was unreliable on stage. He closes by urging developers to validate all input, including sensor data, and to protect firmware and serial interfaces on devices.

talks.title: Goa 2015: Inaugural Note by Shri Janardhana Swamy
talks.teaser: A former parliamentarian frames catastrophic cyber risk and urges secure-by-design policy together with the security research community.
talks.summary:
The inaugural address opens by welcoming attendees and stressing knowledge sharing across organizations and countries. The speaker sketches a career path from Silicon Valley engineering through Indian industry, then five years in Parliament after contesting the 2009 election, noting how long-standing tools and habits in computing still shape how practitioners think about risk.

Drawing on public life, the speaker argues that history repeatedly neared catastrophe through technological mistakes and human error, citing events from the Cuban Missile Crisis through later decades. One individual’s error could now harm a nation or worse, so survival may depend less on perfect defenses than on attackers not having exploited existing weaknesses. The industry’s build-test-ship habit keeps security only as strong as tests; robustness should come from architecture and design instead of ever-bigger locks, with parallels drawn to physical security and social deterrence in places like California.

Government, industry, and the conference community must work together so electronic security evolves beyond algorithms alone. Cyber terrorism could rival nuclear war in impact; researchers are not mere hobbyists but partners policymakers must enable. The Make in India initiative should weave logical and policy dimensions alongside manufacturing, and the gathering is framed as a venue for safer nations and a safer planet.

talks.title: Goa 2014: Hardware Badge 101 Desi Jugaad by Amey & Umesh
talks.teaser: Shows how a microcontroller conference badge was designed, from chip choice and puzzles to PCB layout and mass production.
talks.summary:
It covers the design of a general-purpose hardware badge built for a security conference. The speakers chose an ATmega8 microcontroller for its low cost and low operating voltage, so newcomers would not lose expensive parts to mistakes. The badge carries LEDs, a buzzer, input switches and a USB programming interface, and it is programmed in C and loaded with avrdude. Attendees received puzzle levels, including an EMF detector circuit and a persistence-of-vision display that revealed a Morse code message.

The speakers traced the development history. Early ideas such as IR communication between badges were dropped because of cost and time, and the first prototype carried a temperature sensor, light sensor and LCD. Their problems included a local supplier's USB programmer with swapped MISO and MOSI connections, and an LED that broke during assembly. For PCB layout they advised fixing the concept first, leaving test points, spacing tracks generously, using few jumpers and checking the manufacturer's limits.

For production runs of several hundred units, they advised adding schedule buffer, avoiding reliance on small suppliers for stock, and planning around holidays such as Chinese New Year, which shut suppliers for about two weeks. They also showed how the same chip could drive sensors, relays and IR remotes for home automation, while cautioning that car RF brute forcing would be limited by random number generation. The talk ended with puzzle results: few attendees solved every level, and the top solver won a free pass to the next event.
