talks.title: Goa 2014:- Multi-value WiFi What the Heck is it by Abhijeet Ghosh @Airtight
talks.teaser: Surveys Wi-Fi threats such as rogue access points and evil twins, plus the enterprise controls meant to contain them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why Wi-Fi is attractive to enterprises: it is unlicensed, inexpensive and nearly everywhere, which also invites research and abuse. The speaker argues that the core problem is visibility, since wireless signals leave the building and administrators often cannot see which devices occupy their airspace. Compliance regimes such as PCI and RBI guidelines push organisations to secure their networks, yet open access points remain common in major Indian cities, according to a war-driving scan the speaker mentions.

The middle section walks through threat categories. Rogue access points are described as the most common problem, including a laptop turned into an access point and bridged to a corporate network. Hiding an SSID offers no protection, because clients reveal it during association. Evil twin attacks lure devices that auto-connect to the strongest known network, as with a fake airport hotspot. Other cases include misconfigured or stolen access points, unauthorised client association, ad hoc connections, and an anecdote where handheld gaming devices in ad hoc mode let people coordinate inside a facility.

The closing part argues that accurately classifying devices as authorised, rogue or external is the foundation of wireless intrusion prevention. Modern products combine access and prevention in one package, while security-focused agencies still prefer an overlay design. Bring-your-own-device management is presented as a problem the industry is still maturing around. The talk ends with a feature overview covering guest Wi-Fi analytics and remote troubleshooting.

talks.title: Goa 2014:- Exhibition -Where the industry meets
talks.teaser: Vendors at the exhibition pitch network anomaly detection, vulnerability management, penetration testing and code scanning products.
talks.summary:
This exhibition session is a series of short vendor presentations, each introducing a company's security products rather than a single research talk. One presenter describes a cybersecurity product that uses machine learning and clustering on high-speed network traffic and generated metadata to flag malware and suspicious users before an attack lands, helping analysts contain threats inside the network. Another company describes a security portfolio built around cyber range and attack simulation, using a breaking point appliance to run a range of simulated attacks for customers.

The next segments cover offerings associated with Rapid7. One is a vulnerability analysis product that covers detecting and recording weaknesses and then providing remediation. The other is Metasploit, presented as a penetration testing tool for checking systems against attackers before they act. A further vendor presents a vulnerability management product that scans endpoints, applies fixes, and recommends device hardening. Its argument is that antivirus alone is not enough and that defense in depth needs a first layer of vulnerability management.

The final presenter, from CheckMarks, describes automated source code scanning across multiple languages, aimed at web applications built in India and used by developers. The product reports findings, including high-risk SQL injection issues, and groups related vulnerabilities so that fixing one shared node can clear many findings at once. The presenter closes by saying this was the company's first year exhibiting at the conference and that they hope to return.

talks.title: Goa 2014: ShoulderSurfing 2 0 by Federico Pacheco
talks.teaser: Covers mirror-and-phone shoulder surfing, then frame extraction or Kinovea tracking to infer passwords from short typing videos.
talks.summary:
The presentation revisits classic shoulder surfing by standing roughly a meter from someone logging in, aiming a tiny mirror or periscope at the keyboard with a phone camera, and recording a short clip instead of attacking the network or planting malware. The speaker outlines three ways to recover what was typed: stepping through extracted frames in image editors, preferred inline work in the open-source Kinovea sports tracker, and largely manual fingertip tracking that he treats as out of reach for now.

On a case study with an iPhone 5 under poor light, he overlays keys and compares successive frames to spot which character dips when fingers cross. Kinovea allows flip, rotate, contrast tweaks, grids, and point tracks exported to XML, though full automation fails when keyboard layout and angle change between recordings. A demo slows a few-second mirror capture until the password is obvious; a second clip shows a university friend entering a phone PIN from about two meters after a mistyped attempt.

He notes the method only became practical as phone cameras improved a few years before the talk, and that Indian developers could not fully automate 3D hand modeling yet. The closing argument is privacy hygiene: passwords are often entered in plain view at offices, shielding matters, and the same optics can target phones or electronic locks—practice made colleagues hide keyboards after a prior party demo.

talks.title: Goa 2014:- Fuzzing the easy way using Zulu by Andy Davis
talks.teaser: Shows Zulu, a Burp-style GUI fuzzer that mutates captured network, file and USB traffic and emails proof-of-concept crash scripts.
talks.summary:
Andy Davis presents Zulu, a fuzzer his team built internally and now releases publicly. It is written in Python with a wxPython interface and is modelled on web proxies such as Burp, so testers can capture a legitimate client talking to a server, mark fields for mutation, and replay altered traffic. The tool is mutation-based and currently fuzzes only from client to server. Mutators draw on the open source fuzzing database, extended with the team's own additions.

The talk walks through the main modules. A network proxy captures traffic, and sessions can also be imported from pcap files or Wireshark streams. A file fuzzer launches a chosen application with mutated inputs and runs basic crash triage in a debugger. Specialised modules cover USB devices through a generator script for a USB analyser, and AT commands over serial. Length fields can be recalculated automatically for each test case, and Wireshark can dissect captured data. When a fuzz run stops responding, it pauses rather than ending, and it generates a Python proof-of-concept for the suspected crash case.

VM integration can restart a virtual machine or process after a crash, and email alerts deliver the proof-of-concept scripts. Zulu Script, a custom.py hook, lets users add authentication or encoding between mutation and sending. The speaker reports that the tool has found many bugs in internal research and client work, some already reported and fixed, and points listeners to the GitHub release and the accompanying white paper tutorials.

talks.title: Goa 2014:- Evil Twin Detection by Rushikesh & Amrita
talks.teaser: Presents a user-side method that injects crafted packets to expose evil twin access points copying a legitimate Wi-Fi network.
talks.summary:
The talk examines evil twin attacks on Wi-Fi, where a rogue access point copies a legitimate network's name or MAC address so that a client's traffic can be intercepted or redirected. Open hotspots in airports, cafés and libraries are common targets, and the attack is hard to notice because rogue access points appear and disappear. The speakers cover background on monitor mode and on the probe and beacon frames that advertise networks.

The core of the session is a detection method the speakers devised that runs on the user's own machine. A client in monitor mode sends a crafted TCP packet with the FIN flag set to a suspect access point. In their tests a legitimate AP answers with a RST, while the rogue one stays silent. They built the tool with Scapy, found that some wireless cards inject reliably, and saw weaker results in a virtualised setup than on a live Linux distribution. They also reviewed other approaches, including RF monitoring against an authorised list, round-trip timing analysis, and a watermark packet method that needs a server on the wired side.

The speakers conclude that an ordinary user can check for a suspicious access point without administrator rights. They note that mobile hotspots, and separating true evil twins from legitimate third-party hotspots, remain open problems, and they mention that the work has been filed for a patent. The practical takeaway is that users can test access points themselves, but reliable evil twin detection is still difficult.

talks.title: Goa 2014: Pentesting Proprietary RF Communications by Justin Searle @meeas
talks.teaser: Shows how to find, capture and decode proprietary radio frequency signals used by control systems and wireless devices.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces penetration testing of radio frequency links used by control systems and simple wireless devices. The speaker lists examples such as fire alarm links, proximity cards, gate remotes and hospital beds, and points to the NESCOR testing guide with its 56 tasks. He also stresses that live control systems can fail, so tests must be planned safely.

Next he walks through the radio workflow. Signals can be located using vendor documentation, FCC filings, patents and ISM band tables, such as 915 MHz in the United States and 868 MHz in Europe. Capture options range from low-cost receivers to software-defined radios and RFCAT-based chips. In a live demo, a development watch transmits to an access point, and a GNU Radio flowgraph with a spectrum view, low-pass filter and GFSK decoder isolates the signal and saves a raw bitstream. Frequency hopping is shown to offer little protection once its algorithm is known.

The closing section covers what follows capture. A raw bitstream gives no packet boundaries, so the analyst must find sync words or access keys and correlate them with transmitted test signals. Recovered traffic can then be replayed to check whether a device accepts a recorded stop command or enforces replay protection.

talks.title: Goa 2014: O Dea Assertions Untwining the Security of the SAML protocol by Achin Kulshrestha
talks.teaser: Explains how SAML single sign-on works and how signature wrapping and XML attacks can break SAML service providers.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces SAML, the XML-based standard that lets a company's identity provider vouch for users to cloud and web services, so people do not need a separate password for each application. It walks through a typical web single sign-on flow, where a service provider redirects the browser to the identity provider, which returns a signed assertion carrying authentication, attribute and authorization statements. The speaker explains that the XML signature covers a referenced element rather than the assertion's content directly, which sets up the main weakness.

The central attack covered is signature wrapping. Signature validation finds the signed element by its ID, while claim processing reads values through XPath, so an attacker can move a genuine signed assertion into a wrapper element and place a forged assertion where the claims are read. Other issues include missing schema validation, XML external entity injection through DOCTYPE declarations, and trusting certificates embedded in the key info element without checking them against a trust chain or revocation status.

Countermeasures include rejecting DOCTYPEs, validating each assertion against the SAML schema, and confirming that only the signed element is processed. Keys should be verified before they are trusted. For replay, the talk recommends one-time-use conditions, checking the IssueInstant, rejecting reused request IDs, keeping the NotBefore and NotOnOrAfter window short, and using SubjectLocality. The speaker closes by noting that SAML does not define how an identity provider authenticates users, so that step needs testing as well.

talks.title: Goa 2014: Flowinspect A Network Inspection Tool by Ankur Tyagi @7h3rAm
talks.teaser: Shows Flow Inspect, a Python tool reassembling TCP streams for YARA, fuzzy, regex, and Libemu shellcode detection on captures.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames incident response needs after a compromise: understanding victims, data exposed, lateral movement, exploits, and command-and-control traffic in network captures. Common open-source utilities such as Wireshark, tcpdump, ngrep, and flowgrep are praised for packet capture and decoding but criticized for lacking layer-seven stream awareness, multi-packet pattern matching, malware identification, and on-the-wire shellcode detection.

From that gap the speaker defines requirements for an ideal inspector: signature-based malware detection, shellcode emulation, malware extraction, directional match statistics, custom offsets and depth limits, optional blocking via TCP reset, and stream-level inspection. Flow Inspect is introduced as a Python 2.7 tool with input, inspection, and output modules using libnids for TCP reassembly, BPF filtering, and four modes—regex, fuzzy string matching, Yara, and Libemu shellcode detection with optional API profiling. CLI demos cover HTTP header matching, Adobe Reader CVE-2009-0927 PDF download traffic spanning packets, UPX-packed binaries via Yara, and reverse-shell versus bind-shell shellcode profiles.

Future work includes SMTP and HTTP decoding, file extraction with hash matching, JavaScript de-obfuscation, PDF and JAR validation, and ties to online scanners. The project is open source on GitHub under Creative Commons, built on libnids, Yara, fuzzywuzzy, and Libemu.

talks.title: Goa 2014:-Advanced Smartphone Forensics by Vladimir Katalov @elcomsoft
talks.teaser: Explains how investigators pull data from iPhone, BlackBerry and Windows Phone backups, cloud accounts and keychains.
talks.summary:
The talk, from a password recovery vendor, shows how investigators can pull smartphone data beyond a simple cable connection. It covers iPhone, BlackBerry and Windows Phone; Android was left out of this research. For iOS, the speaker compares logical, advanced logical and physical acquisition, explains that the iTunes backup password is stored on the device, and points out data that survives deletion, such as attachment images, saved Wi-Fi networks and a location history.

The middle section focuses on cloud sources. An iCloud backup can be downloaded with an Apple ID and password, with no handset required, and its chunks were found spread across Amazon and Microsoft storage. Downloads made through this protocol produced no notification to the account owner. iCloud Documents can be fetched and exported to PDF or Office formats, Find My iPhone can return a device's location, and iCloud Keychain was examined, including the SMS verification step that protects it. For BlackBerry, older desktop backups were weakly protected, while BlackBerry 10 backup keys were held by a vendor service. Windows Phone data was reached through Microsoft account interfaces.

The closing point is a trade-off between security, privacy and convenience. Anyone holding cloud credentials may reach far more than the handset itself, and the provider may hold the keys. The speaker lists open work on photo streams, third-party app data and fingerprint data.

talks.title: Goa 2014:- Pentesting without pentesters by Lavakumar, Ankita
talks.teaser: Shows how existing Selenium functional tests can drive automated web vulnerability scans without extra security testing budget.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a problem faced by small development teams that ship frequent releases but cannot afford security testing for each one. The speaker asked whether security checks could be added to the functional testing that already runs on every build, without slowing releases or adding staff. To learn that process, the speaker worked with a functional tester and saw how browser-driven Selenium test cases mimic user actions.

The central idea is to route Selenium test traffic through an intercepting proxy so a scanner records the requests the tests generate. Test cases reach the useful parts of an application and fill in valid data, which automated crawlers often miss. A difficulty was that tests log out at the end, so replaying raw logs would use invalid sessions. The speaker added a start and end call to each test so the scanner groups requests into workflows. It then maps dependencies between requests, such as CSRF tokens taken from earlier responses, and replays them dynamically. In a demo, this approach found a cross-site scripting issue.

The talk also argued that findings should suit developers. Typical penetration test reports describe impact in terms developers do not need, so the speaker proposed step-by-step fix instructions. Encoding recommendations depend on the context where input is reflected, such as HTML or CSS. The reporting component was still in development, and the approach had been tried in one live environment. The takeaway is that teams can reuse existing functional tests for scanning and give developers concrete remediation steps.

talks.title: Goa 2014:- Chrome Security 2014: New and future hotness by Sumit Gwalani
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Goa 2014:- Chrome Security 2014: New and future hotness by Sumit Gwalani.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at Nullcon Goa 2014, Sumit Gwalani of the Chrome security team details recent architectural defenses and future security initiatives across the Chrome browser and Chrome OS. Guided by the core engineering principles of speed, simplicity, and defense-in-depth security, Gwalani highlights how the team mitigates entire vulnerability classes rather than relying on one-off fixes. The talk spans user-space mitigations, kernel-level sandboxing, cryptographic hardware roots of trust, and community vulnerability reward initiatives.

### Key Topics
- **Core Design Principles**: Building transparent, performant security that does not impede UX, treating security as an engineering-wide responsibility, maintaining rapid patch turnaround times (<24 hours), and keeping security designs public.
- **Chrome Browser Mitigations**: Mitigating use-after-free and type confusion vulnerabilities via PartitionAlloc and V8 JavaScript-to-C++ binding integrity checks, cert pinning to Google intermediate CAs, and blocking NPAPI plugins by default.
- **Continuous Testing via ClusterFuzz**: Running automated large-scale fuzzing across hundreds of VMs and thousands of Chrome instances with AddressSanitizer (ASan) to catch memory safety bugs pre-release.
- **Site Isolation**: Developing a site-per-process model to allocate separate sandbox processes to distinct web origins, mitigating cross-site iframe leaks and renderer-initiated navigations beyond basic Same-Origin Policy.
- **Chrome OS Hardware Root of Trust**: Implementing Verified Boot via static read-only firmware, cryptographic signature chains (RSA 8192-bit down to 2048-bit), and kernel `dm-verity` hash trees for block-level execution verification while maintaining sub-10-second boot times.
- **Data Protection & System Hardening**: Employing TPM-backed encryption for user home directories (eCryptfs) and system storage (dm-crypt), sandboxing system daemons using the `minijail` helper, implementing `seccomp-bpf` filters across renderers and GPU processes, and contributing Kernel ASLR (KASLR) upstream to Linux.
- **Vulnerability Rewards Program (VRP)**: Incentivizing researchers through Chromium VRP, Pwnium competitions, and programs paying for open-source patches in core third-party open-source libraries and the Linux kernel.

### Technical Details
- **PartitionAlloc**: Partitions heap allocations by object hierarchy (e.g., dedicated heaps for DOM nodes, Blink/WebKit rendering nodes, and user-controlled buffers like array buffers and strings) isolated with guard pages to prevent cross-object type confusion during use-after-free conditions.
- **Binding Integrity**: Stores unguessable representations of V8 object types inside C++ objects using ASLR defenses; validates wrapper types upon object creation without requiring costly per-call validation overhead.
- **ClusterFuzz**: Automates crash detection, minimizer workflows, and test execution using AddressSanitizer (ASan) builds with poisoned `malloc` and `free` routines, catching over 1,000 vulnerabilities prior to release.
- **Verified Boot & dm-verity**: Boot execution verifies a chain from read-only firmware (8192-bit RSA) to read-write firmware (4096-bit RSA) to the kernel partition (2048-bit RSA). The kernel validates root filesystem blocks on access using a hash tree rooted in a parent hash passed via the kernel command line (`dm-verity`).
- **Storage Encryption**: User home directories are encrypted with 128-bit AES keys wrapped by 512-bit and 2048-bit RSA keys derived jointly from user credentials and the hardware TPM chip, simultaneously providing anti-theft protection and hardware-enforced brute-force rate-limiting.
- **Seccomp-BPF & KASLR**: Employs Berkeley Packet Filter program decision trees to inspect system call numbers and arguments without loops. Used in renderer processes (alongside setuid sandboxing) and GPU processes (via an intercepting helper process). Added x86 Kernel ASLR support by walking e820 memory regions and randomizing boot locations using CPU primitives like `RDRAND`, coupled with restrictions on `dmesg` and kernel pointer leaks.

### Takeaways
Chrome and Chrome OS treat security as an end-to-end systems challenge spanning hardware, kernel primitives, and user-space memory allocators. By introducing structural architectural barriers (like PartitionAlloc, Site Isolation, dm-verity, and seccomp-bpf), attackers must chain together significantly more zero-day vulnerabilities (moving from single-bug exploits to chains of 6 to 14 bugs). The team also actively upstreamed core defenses (such as `dm-verity` and Linux KASLR) and continues to fund external hardening through proactive bug bounties and open-source patch rewards.

talks.title: Goa 2014:- Attacking WPA/WPA2 in the Cloud by Vivek Ramachandran
talks.teaser: Shows how WPA/WPA2 passphrase dictionary attacks can be distributed across cloud instances, with cost figures.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how WPA and WPA2 personal passphrases are checked. The passphrase is run through PBKDF2 together with the network name (SSID) to produce a pairwise master key, which is then verified against a captured four-way handshake using the Michael integrity check. Dictionary attacks remain the standard approach, and the key derivation step is the expensive part, which is why a single laptop manages only tens of thousands of guesses.

The speaker presents a Python tool called Chiju that spreads this work across Amazon EC2 instances or Google App Engine. A master node generates candidate passphrases, workers compute the master keys and store them in a SQL database, and Amazon SQS carries the messages between them. Because most networks never change their SSID, precomputed master keys can be reused against many different handshakes. The benchmarks quoted were about 1000 master keys per second per instance, around 360 million per hour across 100 instances, and roughly 45 billion handshake verifications per hour on the same setup. Enterprise WPA2 with PEAP and MSCHAPv2 was covered as a similar challenge-response problem, once credentials are captured through a rogue access point.

The main takeaway is that short or predictable passphrases are exposed to cloud-scale guessing, and that verification becomes very cheap once keys are precomputed. The speaker said the tool would be released with guidance to build your own machine image and to review the provider terms of service before running it.

talks.summary:
The keynote starts from the observation that security thinking still centers on laptops and desktops, while attacks now reach smart TVs, baby monitors, connected trash cans, point-of-sale terminals, airport X-ray machines and cars. The speaker describes a shift from lone hackers motivated by fame to organized groups driven by financial, political or other clear goals, including state-backed actors and mercenary groups.

The middle section covers advanced persistent threats, with more zero-day vulnerabilities used in recent campaigns and retail breaches that stayed hidden for almost six months before becoming public. Stuxnet is presented as a highly targeted, sophisticated piece of malware that likely required large teams and several zero-days. The speaker walks through the attack lifecycle of reconnaissance, gaining access, discovery, capture and exfiltration, and notes that attackers have used smaller suppliers in Indian cities as stepping stones to larger companies. Patching delays of a few months to almost six months are highlighted as a persistent problem.

The closing advice favors a risk-based approach that puts spending on the most critical assets, layered defenses that protect the data center rather than only the perimeter, and fast response and recovery planning on the assumption that every organization will be attacked. It also calls for public-private collaboration, security intelligence that correlates large volumes of data, and staff education about phishing. Growing data volumes and hybrid cloud environments add further pressure.

talks.title: Goa 2013: A Real Stealth & semi stealth MITM Attack
talks.teaser: Shows a semi-stealth man-in-the-middle method that maps victim IPs to broadcast MACs to hide the attacker's address.
talks.summary:
Traditional ARP-based man-in-the-middle attacks are easy to spot, because the attacker's MAC address is recorded in switch port tables and can be traced back to a physical port. The talk proposes a stealthier variant. The attacker binds each victim's IP address to the broadcast MAC address, so traffic between the two hosts goes to everyone on the segment and the attacker can copy it without any packet carrying the attacker's own hardware address.

A demo in VirtualBox used a Windows victim, a second host and an attacker, with a small Python tool that has a GUI. The operator can start the spoof, inspect the ARP caches of both victims, and undo the poisoning, which sends a burst of corrective ARP packets to restore the original mappings. A semi-stealth mode adds packet modification. When the victim drops frames addressed to broadcast, the attacker re-addresses the packets to the victim's unicast MAC. Against an unsecured host, the attacker can tamper with traffic in both directions, but its MAC address is then exposed.

On detection, a managed switch with ARP inspection can flag ARP replies that map a unicast IP address to a broadcast MAC. That reveals that an attack is happening, but not who is behind it. The speaker reported testing the tool on lab and production networks with 300-plus hosts. For defenders, the takeaway is to alert on any ARP entry that maps a unicast IP to a broadcast address and to treat it as a sign of a stealth attack that needs further investigation.

talks.title: Goa 2013 HTML5 Attack and Defense by Ksenia Dmitrieva
talks.teaser: Shows how HTML5 features like CORS, postMessage, web storage and iframe sandboxing create attack paths, and how to lock them down.
talks.summary:
The talk tours several HTML5 features and how each one gets misused, noting that the specification is still evolving. It starts with cross-origin resource sharing, where a wildcard allowed-origin header lets any site read responses meant for a trusted domain. The speaker recommends listing exact origins, keeping the cache lifetime short, and remembering that the setting applies to the whole site rather than individual paths.

Cross-document messaging comes next. A parent page that accepts messages from an iframe without checking the sender's origin can be fed script by an untrusted frame, demonstrated with a malicious link injected into the page. The fixes covered are checking the origin, validating that the data matches the expected format, and writing output with text content instead of inner HTML. Web storage is then discussed: values in local and session storage stay readable on the machine and are shared across application paths on one domain, so sensitive data should be avoided or cleared after use. Finally, the sandbox attribute on iframes is examined, where an empty value blocks scripts and DOM access, while looser values can reopen clickjacking. Frame-busting JavaScript was shown being bypassed, and a CSS-based approach that hides the page until it confirms it is the top frame was offered as a sturdier defence.

The closing remarks point to other features such as WebSockets and geolocation, which raise their own transport and privacy concerns. The practical takeaway is to check browser support for any new API, consider how an attacker could abuse it, and research its security implications before adopting it.

talks.title: Goa 2013 - Inception of graphical passwords
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Goa 2013 - Inception of graphical passwords - By Rishi Narang.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Nullcon Goa 2013, Rishi introduces the concept and proof-of-concept implementation of graphical passwords for web applications, inspired by connect-the-dots games and touchscreen gestures. The motivation stems from the difficulty of typing complex, lengthy alphanumeric passwords on touch-enabled devices and the tendency of users to forget complex credentials. Rishi discusses how graphical pattern passwords can improve usability while mitigating conventional password guessing and simple network credential sniffing.

### Key Topics
- **Issues with Conventional Passwords**: Alphanumeric passwords require remembering words and phrases, which makes complex passwords easy to forget or leads users to pick guessable passwords. Typing long credentials with special characters is especially tedious on mobile and touchscreen interfaces.
- **Limitations of Existing Android Pattern Locks**: Traditional Android 3x3 pattern locks enforce strict constraints: users cannot lift their fingers, cannot draw disjoint parallel lines, cannot click the same dot repeatedly, and cannot connect fewer than a minimum threshold of dots.
- **Connect-the-Dots Concept**: Rishi's approach allows lifting the finger, repeating clicks on the same node, drawing parallel segments, and freely scaling the grid (e.g., 3x3, 4x4, 6x6, or non-grid arbitrary dot distributions).
- **Visual Feedback and Usability**: Using HTML5 Canvas or plain CSS, the interface provides visual feedback, such as color changes corresponding to the number of clicks on each dot.
- **Obfuscation Against Man-in-the-Middle (MITM)**: By dynamically generating random session-specific keys on the server and binding them to each grid point, sniffers looking strictly for static password parameters fail to capture reusable credentials unless the complete initial session payload is intercepted.

### Technical Details
- **Grid Representation and Sessions**: During registration, dot positions (e.g., coordinates numbered 11 through 22 in a grid) are recorded as the pattern sequence. At authentication time, the server generates unique random numbers for each dot (ensuring no duplicates) and stores them temporarily in a `session_tab` database table. These numbers are passed to the client JavaScript.
- **Credential Transmission**: When the user clicks or connects dots, the client sends the assigned random session values instead of the raw dot IDs. The backend maps the received random tokens back to the dot identifiers via an array lookup to verify against the stored pattern in `user_pass`.
- **Complex Strings via Predefined Values**: Rishi demonstrates that clicking dots can also append multi-character strings with symbols (such as alphanumeric substrings) to form a high-entropy string automatically from simple geometric inputs.
- **Weaknesses and Mitigations**: A major limitation is shoulder surfing or surveillance via CCTV. Rishi explores potential counter-measures, such as disabling visual cues or experimenting with deceptive/false color feedbacks.

### Takeaways & Future Roadmap
Graphical passwords serve as an accessible primary authentication method or as an additional authentication step for web platforms. Rishi outlines ongoing and planned developments, including a WordPress authentication plugin, true HTML5 path/line drawing, mathematical color-palette fill grids, handwriting/signature dot-density analysis, and a follow-up paper focused on testing and attacking graphical password schemes.

talks.teaser: Introduces an open-source pentest distribution and methodology for smart grid and control system environments.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Samurai STFU, a freely available open-source penetration testing distribution aimed at electric utilities and other control system environments. The speaker explains why testing these networks needs special care: a careless port scan, spider, or automated vulnerability scan aimed at a control server can crash equipment, interrupt power to a substation, or halt a production line. Field devices in substations and plants are also reachable by physical attackers, so the testing scope has to extend down to embedded hardware and not stop at the servers.

The middle of the talk covers the toolset and methodology. The distribution bundles tools for JTAG and serial bus work, bus snooping, firmware disassembly, software-defined radio and custom wireless protocols, and fuzzers and simulators for industrial protocols. Practical cautions include slowing port scans, avoiding empty UDP probes that some control protocols cannot handle, and using a Nessus policy that favors authenticated checks over unauthenticated ones. For proprietary protocols, the speaker described reverse engineering only as much as needed to fuzz a target, and gave rough effort estimates for embedded and wireless work.

The closing portion covered the release plan, documentation, and training. The speaker said the public release would follow within a few weeks, with a mailing list for feedback, and that commercial support would be offered as services rather than as a separate paid edition. A practitioner should take away that control environments need context-aware testing: check protocol behavior and device fragility before running standard tools, and treat physical access to field devices as a real attack path.

talks.title: What Speakers have to say about nullcon Goa!
talks.teaser: Researchers highlight nullcon Goa as a hub for talent, hands-on learning, networking, and raising India's cybersecurity awareness.
talks.summary:
The session collects short reflections on nullcon in Goa from people active in the security field. They describe the event as one of the strongest conferences globally and in India, citing enthusiastic crowds, skilled researchers from India and abroad, solid paper sessions, useful workshops, and rich interaction across security communities. For many participants, attending is a way to give back and stay connected with peers who think alike.

A recurring theme is education and practice. Several comments argue that schools alone do not produce capable security professionals; progress comes from sharing knowledge, collaborating openly, and learning in groups. The conference is framed as fun as well as serious—a place to hear new work, meet interesting people, network, and unwind. Speakers also tie the meeting to wider needs in India, including spreading awareness and addressing gaps such as cybersecurity policy.

Later remarks broaden the purpose beyond protocol-centric habits toward a wider view of what security means and how network thinking can matter. The event is characterized as an Indian-rooted security conference that has grown since its start, highlighting local researchers and offering a platform for work and technologies emerging from India rather than simply copying Western models.
